# Overview



PLUMED2 is a molecular dynamics plugin system that provides collective variables and enhanced sampling methods through a modular, extensible framework. The project enables researchers to analyze and bias MD simulations by defining collective variables (CVs) that capture relevant structural and thermodynamic properties of molecular systems. Written primarily in C++ with Python bindings available, PLUMED2 integrates seamlessly with popular MD codes including GROMACS, NAMD, LAMMPS, and Quantum ESPRESSO through a patching mechanism that injects PLUMED functionality directly into these simulation engines.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L50), [developer-doc/Intro.md](/developer-doc/Intro.md#L1-L20)

## Project Purpose and Scope

The core purpose of PLUMED2 is to bridge the gap between molecular dynamics simulations and free energy calculations by providing tools for collective variable analysis, metadynamics, umbrella sampling, and other enhanced sampling techniques. The library operates as a plugin that processes MD trajectory data on-the-fly, applying biases or performing analysis without requiring post-processing of simulation outputs. This real-time approach enables adaptive sampling strategies and immediate feedback during simulations, which is particularly valuable for studying rare events, conformational changes, and phase transitions in complex molecular systems.

![PLUMED Logo](https://github.com/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/user-doc/logo.png?raw=true)

PLUMED2 follows a modular design philosophy where functionality is organized into specialized modules for different types of collective variables (distances, angles, torsions, coordination numbers), biasing methods (metadynamics, restraints, walls), and analysis tools. The current stable release branch is v2.10 with active development continuing on the master branch toward version 2.11. The project maintains strict backward compatibility policies through versioned branches, ensuring that research workflows remain stable across different PLUMED releases.

Sources: [VERSION.txt](/VERSION.txt#L1-L9), [README.md](/README.md#L20-L45)

## Architecture Overview

PLUMED2 employs an **Action-based execution model** where every operation (CV calculation, bias application, analysis) is represented as an Action object that processes data at each simulation timestep. Actions are organized in a hierarchical class structure with the base `Action` class providing common functionality, while specialized classes like `Colvar` (collective variables), `Bias` (biasing methods), and various analysis tools inherit from this foundation. The `PlumedMain` class serves as the central coordinator that manages the Action registry, handles MD code communication, and orchestrates the execution sequence.

```mermaid
graph TB
    MD["MD Engine<br/>GROMACS/NAMD/LAMMPS/QE"] -->|"Patched Interface"| Wrapper["PLUMED Wrapper<br/>C/Fortran Interface"]
    Wrapper --> PlumedMain["PlumedMain<br/>Central Coordinator"]
    PlumedMain --> ActionSet["ActionSet<br/>Action Registry"]
    ActionSet --> Action1["Action Base Class"]
    Action1 --> Colvar["Colvar<br/>Collective Variables"]
    Action1 --> Bias["Bias<br/>Biasing Methods"]
    Action1 --> Analysis["Analysis<br/>Analysis Tools"]
    Action1 --> Tools["Tools<br/>Utility Functions"]
    
    Colvar -->|"Examples"| Distance["Distance"]
    Colvar -->|"Examples"| Angle["Angle"]
    Colvar -->|"Examples"| RMSD["RMSD"]
    
    Bias -->|"Examples"| MetaD["Metadynamics"]
    Bias -->|"Examples"| Restraint["Restraints"]
    Bias -->|"Examples"| Walls["Walls"]
    
    PlumedMain -->|"Module System"| ModuleMap["ModuleMap<br/>Module Registry"]
    ModuleMap --> CoreModules["Core Modules"]
    ModuleMap --> Plugins["Plugins<br/>CUDA/Python"]
    
    style PlumedMain fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
    style Wrapper fill:#bbf,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    
    %% 为部分子节点添加样式以区分层级
    style Action1 fill:#dfd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
    style Colvar fill:#dfd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
    style Bias fill:#dfd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
    style ModuleMap fill:#ffd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
```

The architecture supports **multiple inheritance patterns** through specialized mixin classes (ActionAtomistic, ActionWithValue, ActionWithArguments) that can be combined to create Actions with specific capabilities. This design enables developers to implement new CVs or biasing methods by inheriting from appropriate base classes and overriding specific methods without modifying the core framework. The Action registration system uses factory patterns to dynamically load Actions from modules, allowing for runtime extensibility through shared libraries.

Sources: [src/core/Action.h](/src/core/Action.h#L60-L80), [src/core/PlumedMain.h](/src/core/PlumedMain.h#L70-L90), [src/core/ModuleMap.h](/src/core/ModuleMap.h#L1-L31)

## Repository Structure

The PLUMED2 repository follows a conventional open-source project layout with clear separation between source code, documentation, testing, and integration components. The source code is organized modularly in the `src/` directory, where each subdirectory corresponds to a functional area (core framework, collective variables, biasing methods, analysis tools). This modular organization enables developers to focus on specific functionality areas without needing to understand the entire codebase structure.

```mermaid
graph LR
    Root[plumed2/] --> Src[src/]
    Root --> UserDoc[user-doc/]
    Root --> DevDoc[developer-doc/]
    Root --> Regtest[regtest/]
    Root --> Patches[patches/]
    Root --> Python[python/]
    Root --> Plugins[plugins/]
    Root --> NewManual[new-manual/]
    
    Src --> Core[core/]
    Src --> Colvar[colvar/]
    Src --> Bias[bias/]
    Src --> Analysis[analysis/]
    Src --> Wrapper[wrapper/]
    
    Core --> Action[Action.h/cpp]
    Core --> PlumedMain[PlumedMain.h/cpp]
    Core --> ActionSet[ActionSet.h/cpp]
    
    Colvar --> Distance[Distance.cpp]
    Colvar --> Angle[Angle.cpp]
    Colvar --> RMSD[RMSD.cpp]
    
    Bias --> MetaD[MetaD.cpp]
    Bias --> Restraint[Restraint.cpp]
    
    Patches --> Gromacs[gromacs-*.diff/]
    Patches --> Namd[namd-*.diff]
    Patches --> Qespresso[qespresso-*.diff/]
    
    Plugins --> CUDA[cudaCoord/]
    Plugins --> PythonCV[pycv/]
    
    style Core fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:3px
    style Colvar fill:#bfb,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style Bias fill:#fbf,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
```

The **core module** (`src/core/`) contains the fundamental framework components including the Action hierarchy, PlumedMain coordinator, and utility classes for parallel execution, domain decomposition, and data passing. The **colvar module** (`src/colvar/`) implements various collective variables from simple geometric measurements (distance, angle, dihedral) to complex structural descriptors (RMSD, path-based CVs, coordination numbers). The **bias module** (`src/bias/`) provides enhanced sampling methods including well-tempered metadynamics, bias-exchange metadynamics, restraints, and harmonic/repulsive walls. The **wrapper module** (`src/wrapper/`) contains the C and Fortran interfaces that enable integration with external MD codes.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L50-L80), [src/](/src/), [src/colvar/](/src/colvar/), [src/bias/](/src/bias/)

## Key Components

### Core Framework

The core framework provides the foundation for all PLUMED2 operations through a set of interconnected classes that manage simulation state, coordinate Action execution, and handle MD code communication. The `PlumedMain` class acts as the central orchestrator, maintaining references to all registered Actions and implementing the `cmd()` interface that external MD codes use to interact with PLUMED. The `ActionSet` class manages the collection of Actions, ensuring proper initialization order and execution dependencies. Domain decomposition support enables parallel execution across multiple MPI ranks, with the `DataPassingTools` class handling communication between different simulation domains.

> [!TIP]
> The Action class hierarchy uses virtual inheritance for mixin classes (ActionAtomistic, ActionWithValue, ActionWithArguments) to prevent diamond inheritance problems when combining multiple capabilities in a single Action subclass. This design pattern enables flexible composition of features while maintaining clean object-oriented design principles.

Sources: [src/core/PlumedMain.h](/src/core/PlumedMain.h#L70-L90), [src/core/Action.h](/src/core/Action.h#L60-L80)

### Collective Variables

Collective variables (CVs) represent the computational chemistry domain language of PLUMED2, providing a rich library of structural descriptors that capture essential features of molecular systems. The CV implementation hierarchy extends from the base `Colvar` class, with specialized classes for different types of measurements. Simple geometric CVs include distances, angles, torsions, and coordination numbers, while more complex CVs include root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), path collective variables, and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA). MultiColvar classes enable calculation of CVs over multiple atom groups simultaneously, generating scalar or vector outputs that can be used directly in biasing methods or analysis operations.

| CV Category | Examples | Use Cases |
|-------------|----------|-----------|
| Geometric | Distance, Angle, Dihedral, Coordination | Bond formation, conformational analysis |
| Structural | RMSD, PathMSD, Gyration | Folding pathways, structural similarity |
| Environment | SASA, Packing, Clusters | Solvation effects, protein stability |
| Advanced | ERMSD, PCARMSD, PropertyMap | Complex structural transitions |

Sources: [src/colvar/](/src/colvar/), [src/colvar/Colvar.h](/src/colvar/Colvar.h)

### Biasing Methods

The biasing module implements enhanced sampling techniques that modify the potential energy surface to accelerate exploration of rare events and improve sampling efficiency. The well-tempered metadynamics implementation (`MetaD`) adds Gaussian bias potentials along selected CVs, with the height of the Gaussian scaled by a temperature factor to prevent divergence. Bias-exchange methods enable parallel tempering across different biasing conditions, while umbrella sampling (`Restraint`) provides harmonic restraints to sample specific regions of CV space. Walls (`Walls`, `LWalls`, `UWalls`) create repulsive potentials that constrain sampling within defined boundaries, useful for maintaining stability in enhanced sampling simulations.

> [!TIP]
> Bias classes implement both the force calculation (through derivative methods) and the energy contribution, with the bias energy automatically subtracted during reweighting calculations. This design enables automatic correction of biased distributions to recover unbiased free energy surfaces without manual intervention.

Sources: [src/bias/](/src/bias/), [src/bias/Bias.h](/src/bias/Bias.h)

## Integration with MD Codes

PLUMED2 integrates with external MD engines through a **patching system** that modifies the MD code source to include PLUMED function calls at appropriate points in the simulation loop. The `patches/` directory contains patch files and configuration scripts for multiple MD code versions (GROMACS 2022-2025, NAMD 2.12-2.14, Quantum ESPRESSO 5.0-7.2). The patching process injects PLUMED initialization at simulation startup, CV calculation and force application at each timestep, and finalization at simulation completion. The C/Fortran wrapper layer (`src/wrapper/`) provides stable interfaces that remain constant across PLUMED versions, ensuring that MD codes patched with older PLUMED versions continue to work with newer releases through careful API versioning.

| MD Code | Supported Versions | Integration Method |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|
| GROMACS | 2022.5, 2023.5, 2024.3, 2025.0 | Source patch |
| NAMD | 2.12, 2.13, 2.14 | Source patch |
| LAMMPS | Multiple versions | USER-PLUMED package |
| Quantum ESPRESSO | 5.0.2, 6.2, 7.0, 7.2 | Source patch |

Sources: [patches/](/patches/), [src/wrapper/Plumed.h](/src/wrapper/Plumed.h)

## Documentation and Resources

PLUMED2 maintains comprehensive documentation for both users and developers through separate documentation systems. The **user documentation** (user-doc/) provides reference documentation for all collective variables, biasing methods, and tools, organized by functional area with extensive examples and tutorials. The documentation is generated using Doxygen from annotated source code, with custom layout configuration (PlumedLayout.xml) defining the navigation structure and organization. The **developer documentation** (developer-doc/) contains technical guides for contributing to PLUMED2, including instructions for adding new collective variables, implementing biasing methods, writing regression tests, and understanding the code architecture. The **new manual** (new-manual/) represents a next-generation documentation system using MkDocs with a modern web-based interface.

![Octocat](https://github.com/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/developer-doc/octocat.png?raw=true)

The regression testing framework (regtest/) provides automated validation of PLUMED2 functionality through a collection of test cases covering all major features. Each test directory contains input files, configuration settings, and reference outputs that are compared against new calculations to detect unintended changes. The testing infrastructure supports multiple backends including simplemd (a minimal MD engine for testing), driver (standalone trajectory processing), and integration with external MD codes.

Sources: [user-doc/](/user-doc/), [user-doc/PlumedLayout.xml](/user-doc/PlumedLayout.xml#L1-L50), [developer-doc/](/developer-doc/), [regtest/README](/regtest/README#L1-L50)

## Extension and Customization

PLUMED2 supports extensibility through both built-in module systems and external plugins. The **module system** enables organization of related Actions into logical groups that can be enabled or disabled at compile time through configuration options. Core modules include standard CVs, biasing methods, and analysis tools, while optional modules provide experimental features or dependencies on external libraries. The **plugin system** allows developers to create custom functionality without modifying the PLUMED2 core codebase, with plugins compiled as shared libraries that can be loaded at runtime using the `LOAD` directive.

The `plugins/` directory contains example plugins including CUDA implementations for GPU acceleration (cudaCoord/) and Python interfaces for custom CV implementation (pycv/). These plugins demonstrate the extension patterns for adding new functionality, with build systems (Makefiles, CMakeLists.txt) that integrate with the PLUMED2 build infrastructure. The Python plugin system enables researchers to implement custom CVs using Python syntax, with performance-critical sections handled through Cython compilation to C extensions.

Sources: [plugins/](/plugins/), [src/core/ModuleMap.h](/src/core/ModuleMap.h#L1-L31)

## Getting Started

For developers new to PLUMED2, the recommended learning progression starts with understanding the basic architecture and workflow before diving into specific implementations. Begin by reviewing the [Quick Start](2-quick-start) guide to set up a development environment and compile PLUMED2 from source. Once configured, explore the **Basic Collective Variables** tutorial to understand how CVs are calculated and used. Progress to the **Metadynamics Fundamentals** tutorial to learn about enhanced sampling techniques and how bias potentials modify simulation dynamics.

Developers interested in extending PLUMED2 should proceed to the **Action Framework and Execution Model** documentation to understand the core architecture, then review the **Creating New CVs** and **Creating New Bias Methods** guides for implementation details. The regression testing framework documentation provides guidance on writing tests to validate new functionality, ensuring that contributions maintain code quality and reliability across the evolving codebase.

The PLUMED2 community maintains active discussion forums where developers can ask questions, share experiences, and collaborate on new features. Contributing to PLUMED2 requires understanding the coding standards (documented in CodeFormatting.md), following the contribution guidelines, and ensuring that all changes include appropriate tests and documentation updates.


# Quick Start



This guide provides a fast-track introduction to PLUMED2, designed to get beginners running enhanced molecular dynamics simulations within minutes. PLUMED2 is a plugin that adds advanced free energy methods and collective variable (CV) analysis to popular MD engines like GROMACS, NAMD, LAMMPS, and Quantum ESPRESSO. The current development version is **2.11.0-dev** [Sources: VERSION.txt](VERSION.txt#L1-L9).

## System Architecture

Understanding how PLUMED integrates with MD engines is fundamental to effective usage. The system operates as a **modular enhancement layer** that intercepts simulation steps to calculate CVs, apply biases, and analyze trajectories.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "MD Engine (GROMACS/NAMD/LAMMPS/QE)"
        MD[MD Simulation Core]
        Atoms[Atomic Positions]
        Forces[Force Calculations]
    end
    
    subgraph "PLUMED Interface Layer"
        PL[Plumed Wrapper]
        API[Plumed.h Interface]
    end
    
    subgraph "PLUMED Core"
        CV[Collective Variables<br/>DISTANCE, ANGLE, TORSION]
        Bias[Biasing Methods<br/>METAD, RESTRAINT]
        Analysis[Analysis Tools<br/>PRINT, HISTOGRAM]
        Action[Action Registry]
    end
    
    MD -->|Atomic positions| PL
    PL -->|CV values| CV
    CV -->|Bias forces| Bias
    Bias -->|Additional forces| PL
    PL -->|Modified forces| Forces
    
    MD <-->|API calls| API
    API --> PL
    
    PL --> Action
    Action --> CV
    Action --> Bias
    Action --> Analysis
    
    style PL fill:#e1f5ff
    style CV fill:#fff4e1
    style Bias fill:#ffe1e1
    style Analysis fill:#e1ffe1
```

PLUMED follows an **action-based execution model** where each input directive creates an Action object. These actions are organized in a dependency graph and executed at appropriate simulation steps. The core architecture supports three integration modes: **static linking**, **shared library**, and **runtime loading** [Sources: developer-doc/Intro.md](developer-doc/Intro.md#L63-L95).

## Installation Methods

PLUMED offers multiple installation approaches tailored to different user needs and system configurations.

### Method 1: Source Compilation (Recommended for Developers)

Source compilation provides maximum flexibility and is the primary method for developers and users requiring custom configurations.

**Prerequisites:**
- GNU make
- C/C++ compiler with C++17 support (required as of version 2.10)
- Modern `patch` command-line tool
- Suggested libraries: auto-detected by configure script [Sources: README.md](README.md#L67-L80)

**Compilation workflow:**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Download Source] --> B[./configure<br/>Detect system & libraries]
    B --> C[make -j N<br/>Compile source code]
    C --> D[make install<br/>Install to system]
    D --> E[source setup.sh<br/>Set environment variables]
    
    style B fill:#e3f2fd
    style C fill:#fff3e0
    style D fill:#e8f5e9
```

**Basic commands:**

```bash
# Configure with default settings
./configure

# Compile with parallel jobs (N = number of CPU cores)
make -j 8

# Install to configured prefix (default: /usr/local)
sudo make install

# Set up environment variables
source /path/to/plumed/sourceme.sh
```

The configuration script creates `Makefile.conf` with system-specific settings including compiler flags, library paths, and module configurations [Sources: Makefile.conf.in](Makefile.conf.in#L1-L50). Advanced users can enable specific modules or MPI support using configure options.

### Method 2: Package Managers

For production environments, pre-built packages offer faster deployment with tested dependencies:

| Package Manager | Command | Notes |
|----------------|---------|-------|
| Conda | `conda install -c conda-forge plumed` | Cross-platform, includes Python interface |
| MacPorts | `sudo port install plumed` | macOS optimized [Sources: README.md](README.md#L14-L15) |
| Spack | `spack install plumed` | HPC environment friendly |

![PLUMED badges](https://github.com/plumed/plumed2/raw/master/README.md) [Sources: README.md](README.md#L1-L16)

### Method 3: Container Deployment

Docker provides reproducible environments ideal for testing and cloud deployment:

```bash
# Build from Dockerfile
cd docker
make

# Run PLUMED container
docker run -it plumed:latest bash
```

The docker directory includes configurations for multiple distributions (Fedora 39, Rocky 8) with Python CV support options [Sources: docker/Dockerfile](docker/Dockerfile).

### Installation Validation

Verify your installation with:

```bash
# Check PLUMED version
plumed info --version

# List available CVs and actions
plumed info --action-list

# Test with simple example
cd test/gromacs
# (requires GROMACS installation)
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L67-L80), [VERSION.txt](VERSION.txt#L1-L9)

## Your First PLUMED Input File

PLUMED uses a simple, declarative syntax where each line defines an action or calculation. The typical workflow involves defining collective variables, applying biases, and outputting results.

### Basic Syntax Example

Create a file named `plumed.dat`:

```plumed
# Define a distance CV between atoms 1 and 10
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,10

# Print CV value to file
PRINT ARG=d FILE=colvar.dat STRIDE=10
```

This simple input demonstrates PLUMED's core concepts:

1. **CV Definition**: `d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,10` creates a CV named "d" calculating the distance between atoms 1 and 10
2. **Output**: `PRINT ARG=d` writes the CV value to `colvar.dat` every 10 simulation steps
3. **Naming Convention**: Labels like `d:` allow CVs to be referenced by other actions [Sources: test/gromacs/plumed.dat](test/gromacs/plumed.dat#L1-L4)

### Enhanced Example with Metadynamics

A more realistic example adds enhanced sampling:

```plumed
# CV: distance between two atoms
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,10

# Well-tempered metadynamics
METAD ARG=d SIGMA=0.1 HEIGHT=1.0 PACE=100 TEMP=300.0 \
      FILE=HILLS RESTART

# Output CV and bias
PRINT ARG=d,metad.bias FILE=colvar.dat STRIDE=10
```

> [!TIP]
> The METAD directive's RESTART option allows simulations to resume from previous HILLS files, crucial for long enhanced sampling runs. The bias potential is stored and can be analyzed afterward for free energy reconstruction.

**Key parameters explained:**

| Parameter | Meaning | Typical Values |
|-----------|---------|----------------|
| ARG | CV(s) to bias | Comma-separated CV labels |
| SIGMA | Gaussian width (CV units) | ~0.1-0.3 for distances |
| HEIGHT | Initial hill height | 0.5-2.0 kJ/mol |
| PACE | Steps between hills | 100-1000 |
| TEMP | Temperature (K) | Simulation temperature |
| FILE | Output file | HILLS for bias history |

Sources: [test/gromacs/plumed.dat](test/gromacs/plumed.dat#L1-L8)

## Running PLUMED with MD Engines

PLUMED integrates with MD engines through two primary approaches: **patching** (modifying MD source code) and **runtime linking** (using the MD engine's plugin interface).

### Integration Approaches

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Patching Method"
        P1[Apply patch.sh] --> P2[Recompile MD code]
        P2 --> P3[Static PLUMED integration]
    end
    
    subgraph "Runtime Linking"
        R1[Load PLUMED library] --> R2[API calls from MD]
        R2 --> R3[Dynamic CV evaluation]
    end
    
    subgraph "Standalone Mode"
        S1[C++ API] --> S2[Custom simulation loop]
        S2 --> S3[Full PLUMED control]
    end
    
    style P3 fill:#ffebee
    style R3 fill:#e8f5e9
    style S3 fill:#fff3e0
```

### GROMACS Integration Example

**Option 1: Patching (Recommended)**

```bash
# Navigate to PLUMED patches directory
cd /path/to/plumed/patches

# Patch GROMACS (interactive engine selection)
./patch.sh --patch --engine=gromacs

# Recompile GROMACS
cd /path/to/gromacs
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DGMX_BUILD_OWN_FFTW=ON
make -j 8
```

The patch script creates symbolic links to PLUMED headers and modifies the MD code to call PLUMED at each step [Sources: patches/patch.sh](patches/patch.sh#L1-L50).

**Option 2: Runtime Linking**

```bash
# Configure PLUMED as shared library
./configure --enable-shared
make -j 8
sudo make install

# Run GROMACS with PLUMED
gmx mdrun -s topol.tpr -nsteps 100000 -plumed plumed.dat
```

### Standalone C++ Program

For maximum control, you can link PLUMED directly into custom code:

```cpp
#include "plumed/wrapper/Plumed.h"
#include <cstdio>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  PLMD::Plumed plumed;
  const char* input = "plumed.dat";
  
  // Configure PLUMED
  plumed.cmd("setMDEngine", "specific");
  plumed.cmd("setLog", stdout);
  
  // Set simulation details
  int natoms = 20;
  plumed.cmd("setNatoms", &natoms);
  plumed.cmd("setPlumedDat", input);
  plumed.cmd("init");
  
  // Simulation loop
  for(int step = 0; step < 1000; step++) {
    // Update atomic positions (your MD code here)
    // plumed.cmd("setStep", &step);
    // plumed.cmd("setPositions", positions);
    // plumed.cmd("setMasses", masses);
    
    // Calculate bias forces
    // plumed.cmd("calc");
    
    // Get modified forces
    // plumed.cmd("getBias", &energy);
    // plumed.cmd("getForces", forces);
  }
  
  return 0;
}
```

This approach gives you complete control over when PLUMED is called and how forces are applied [Sources: test/link/main.cpp](test/link/main.cpp#L1-L39).

Sources: [patches/patch.sh](patches/patch.sh#L1-L50), [test/link/main.cpp](test/link/main.cpp#L1-L39)

## Supported MD Engines

PLUMED provides patches and integration scripts for multiple MD codes:

| MD Engine | Patch Location | Linking Modes |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| GROMACS | patches/gromacs-2024.3.diff | static, shared, runtime |
| NAMD | patches/namd-2.14.diff | static |
| LAMMPS | patches directory | runtime |

**List available engines:**

```bash
./patch.sh --list-engines
```

Each patch includes a `.config` file with version information and a `.diff/` directory with source modifications [Sources: patches/](patches/gromacs-2024.3.config).

## Testing Your Installation

PLUMED includes regression tests to verify correct operation:

```bash
# Run basic tests
cd test/gromacs
make test

# Run full regression suite
cd regtest
make test
```

The test directory contains example inputs for different MD codes. For GROMACS, you can try:

```bash
cd test/gromacs
# Prepare simulation
gmx grompp -f grompp.mdp -c conf.gro -p topol.top -o md.tpr

# Run with PLUMED
gmx mdrun -s md.tpr -plumed plumed.dat

# Analyze output
# colvar.dat contains CV values over time
```

The regression tests verify that CVs and biases produce correct results across supported engines [Sources: test/Makefile](test/Makefile), [regtest/README](regtest/README).

## Common Troubleshooting

**Issue**: "undefined reference to `plumed_*`"

**Solution**: Ensure PLUMED is compiled as a shared library (`./configure --enable-shared`) and the library path is in `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` [Sources: Makefile.conf.in](Makefile.conf.in#L25-L28).

**Issue**: "Action DISTANCE not found"

**Solution**: Verify PLUMED is properly initialized with `plumed.cmd("init")` after setting all parameters [Sources: test/link/main.cpp](test/link/main.cpp#L22-L25).

**Issue**: Patch fails with "cannot apply patch"

**Solution**: Check MD engine version matches patch version. Use `./patch.sh --info --engine=gromacs` to see supported versions [Sources: patches/patch.sh](patches/patch.sh#L1-L50).

# Basic Collective Variables



This page introduces the fundamental collective variables (CVs) in PLUMED that enable you to reduce the complexity of molecular systems from thousands of atomic coordinates to a handful of meaningful descriptors. These basic CVs serve as building blocks for understanding chemical processes and implementing enhanced sampling techniques.

## Understanding Collective Variables

![PLUMED Overview](https://github.com/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/user-doc/logo.png?raw=true)

Molecular systems contain an enormous number of atoms, making it impossible to understand anything by monitoring atom positions directly. Collective variables (CVs) describe the chemical processes we're interested in and allow us to monitor these simpler quantities instead. CVs are used throughout PLUMED—monitoring them with `PRINT`, calculating functions using the `function` module, analyzing with tools like `dimred` and `gridtools`, or biasing using the `bias` module. Before any of these operations, you must first tell PLUMED how to calculate these variables.

Sources: [module.md](src/colvar/module.md#L1-L16), [GettingStartedPP.md](user-doc/basic.list#L4)

## CV Architecture and Design

The collective variable module provides implementations of the simplest CVs that take a set of atomic positions and output one or multiple scalar CV values. However, the `colvar` module does not contain implementations of all collective variables available in PLUMED—many other modules contain additional CV implementations.

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[PLUMED CV System] --> B[Basic CVs - colvar module]
    A --> C[Path CVs - pathcv module]
    A --> D[Multi-component CVs - multicolvar module]
    A --> E[Secondary Structure - secondarystructure module]
    
    B --> B1[DISTANCE]
    B --> B2[ANGLE]
    B --> B3[TORSION]
    B --> B4[COORDINATION]
    B --> B5[GYRATION]
    B --> B6[RMSD]
    B --> B7[POSITION]
    B --> B8[DIHEDRAL_CORRELATION]
    
    B1 --> F[Used for biasing]
    B1 --> G[Used for analysis]
    B1 --> H[Used for monitoring]
```

The basic CVs all inherit from the `Colvar` base class and are registered through the Action framework, which allows them to be called directly from PLUMED input files using their registered keywords.

Sources: [module.md](src/colvar/module.md#L1-L16), [Colvar.h](src/colvar/Colvar.h#L1-L33)

## Distance-based Collective Variables

### DISTANCE

The `DISTANCE` CV calculates distances between pairs of atoms. This is one of the most fundamental CVs and serves as a building block for many analyses.

**Basic Usage**:
```plumed
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2
PRINT ARG=d FILE=colvar
```

**Key Features**:

| Feature | Description | Example Syntax |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| PBC Handling | Accounts for periodic boundaries by default | Use `NOPBC` to disable |
| Vector Components | Output x,y,z components of the distance vector | `COMPONENTS` flag |
| Scaled Components | Project on lattice vectors with proper periodicity | `SCALED_COMPONENTS` flag |
| Multiple Pairs | Calculate multiple distances in one command | `ATOMS1=`, `ATOMS2=`, etc. |

**Advanced Examples**:

Calculate multiple indistinguishable distances:
```plumed
d: DISTANCE ATOMS1=1,2 ATOMS2=3,4 ATOMS3=5,6 ATOMS4=7,8
PRINT ARG=d FILE=colvar
```

Calculate vector components:
```plumed
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2 COMPONENTS
PRINT ARG=d.x,d.y,d.z FILE=colvar
```

Use scaled components for membrane transport studies (ensures proper periodicity):
```plumed
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2 SCALED_COMPONENTS
PRINT ARG=d.a,d.b,d.c FILE=colvar
```

Sources: [Distance.cpp](src/colvar/Distance.cpp#L35-L100), [Distance.cpp](src/colvar/Distance.cpp#L89-L100), [regtest rt1](regtest/basic/rt1/plumed.dat#L1-L8)

### ANGLE

The `ANGLE` CV calculates angles between vectors. This can involve three atoms (angle at vertex) or four atoms (angle between two vectors).

**Mathematical Definition**:
For three atoms (i, j, k):
$$\theta=\arccos\left(\frac{ r_{ij}\cdot r_{jk}}{| r_{ij}| | r_{jk}|}\right)$$

For four atoms (i, j, k, l):
$$\theta=\arccos\left(\frac{ r_{ji}\cdot r_{kl}}{| r_{ji}| | r_{kl}|}\right)$$

**Basic Usage**:
```plumed
a1: ANGLE ATOMS=1,2,3
PRINT ARG=a1 FILE=colvar
```

**Important Notes**: Angles are non-periodic variables with values between 0 and π. By default, PLUMED ensures atom sets are not broken by periodic boundaries using a procedure similar to `WHOLEMOLECULES`.

**Multiple Angles**:
```plumed
a3: ANGLE ATOMS1=1,2,3 ATOMS2=4,5,6 ATOMS3=7,8,9
PRINT ARG=a3 FILE=colvar
```

Sources: [Angle.cpp](src/colvar/Angle.cpp#L34-L98)

### TORSION

The `TORSION` CV calculates torsional (dihedral) angles involving four atoms, which are essential for studying protein backbone conformations and molecular rotations.

**Standard Usage**:
```plumed
t: TORSION ATOMS=1,2,3,4
PRINT ARG=t FILE=COLVAR
```

**Vector-Plane Projection Syntax**:
```plumed
t: TORSION VECTORA=2,1 AXIS=2,3 VECTORB=3,4 COSINE
PRINT ARG=t FILE=COLVAR
```

This calculates the cosine of the torsion angle, which can be useful in certain applications.

**Protein Structure Integration**: When working with proteins, you can specify special named torsion angles (φ, ψ, ω, χ₁) using the `MOLINFO` command:

```plumed
MOLINFO MOLTYPE=protein STRUCTURE=helix.pdb
t1: TORSION ATOMS=@phi-3
t2: TORSION ATOMS=@psi-4
PRINT ARG=t1,t2 FILE=colvar STRIDE=10
```

Here, `@phi-3` calculates the φ angle in residue 3, and `@psi-4` calculates the ψ angle in residue 4.

**Multiple Torsions**:
```plumed
MOLINFO MOLTYPE=protein STRUCTURE=helix.pdb
t1: TORSION ATOMS1=@phi-3 ATOMS2=@phi-4 ATOMS3=@phi-5 ATOMS4=@phi-6 ATOMS5=@phi-7
PRINT ARG=t1 FILE=colvar STRIDE=10
```

Sources: [Torsion.cpp](src/colvar/Torsion.cpp#L35-L100), [regtest rt32](regtest/basic/rt32/plumed.dat#L1-L5)

### DIHEDRAL_CORRELATION

This CV measures the correlation between pairs of dihedral angles, useful for studying coupled motions in biomolecules.

**Mathematical Definition**:
$$s = \frac{1}{2} \left[ 1 + \cos( \phi - \psi ) \right]$$

**Usage**:
```plumed
d: DIHEDRAL_CORRELATION ATOMS=1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
PRINT ARG=d FILE=colvar
```

This calculates the correlation between the dihedral involving atoms 1-4 (φ) and atoms 5-8 (ψ). The output ranges from 0 (completely uncorrelated) to 1 (perfectly correlated).

**Multiple Pairs**:
```plumed
d: DIHEDRAL_CORRELATION ...
  ATOMS1=1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
  ATOMS2=9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16
...
PRINT ARG=d FILE=colvar
```

Sources: [DihedralCorrelation.cpp](src/colvar/DihedralCorrelation.cpp#L37-L80)

## Coordination and Geometry-based CVs

### COORDINATION

The `COORDINATION` CV calculates the number of contacts between two groups of atoms, which is fundamental for studying solvation, binding, and structural transitions.

**Mathematical Definition**:
$$\sum_{i\in A} \sum_{j\in B} s_{ij}$$

Where $s_{ij}$ is a switching function that provides continuous derivatives:
$$s_{ij} = \frac{ 1 - \left(\frac{r_{ij}-d_0}{r_0}\right)^n } { 1 - \left(\frac{r_{ij}-d_0}{r_0}\right)^m }$$

**Basic Usage**:
```plumed
COORDINATION GROUPA=1-10 GROUPB=20-100 R_0=0.3 NLIST NL_CUTOFF=0.5 NL_STRIDE=100
```

**Key Parameters**:

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `R_0` | Distance cutoff for coordination |
| `NLIST` | Use neighbor list for efficiency |
| `NL_CUTOFF` | Neighbor list cutoff |
| `NL_STRIDE` | Neighbor list update frequency |
| `SWITCH` | Custom switching function |

**Single Group Optimization**: If `GROUPB` is empty, coordination is calculated within `GROUPA`, computing only $\frac{N(N-1)}{2}$ unique pairs rather than $N^2$, doubling the calculation speed.

**Self-interaction Handling**: Since PLUMED 2.1, self-interactions (when GROUPA and GROUPB share atoms) are automatically skipped to count as zero.

Sources: [Coordination.cpp](src/colvar/Coordination.cpp#L29-L96)

### GYRATION

The `GYRATION` CV calculates the radius of gyration, which describes the overall size and compactness of a molecular structure.

**Mathematical Definition**:
$$s_{\rm Gyr}=\Big ( \frac{\sum_i^{n} w_i \vert {r}_i -{r}_{\rm COM} \vert ^2 }{\sum_i^{n} w_i} \Big)^{1/2}$$

With the center of mass position:
$${r}_{\rm COM}=\frac{\sum_i^{n} {r}_i\ w_i }{\sum_i^{n} w_i}$$

**Basic Usage**:
```plumed
g: GYRATION ATOMS=1-5 TYPE=RADIUS
PRINT ARG=g FILE=colvar
```

**Mass-Weighted Calculation**:
```plumed
g: GYRATION ATOMS=1-5 TYPE=RADIUS MASS_WEIGHTED
# Equivalent forms:
g2: GYRATION ATOMS=1-5 TYPE=RADIUS WEIGHTS=@Masses
g3: GYRATION ATOMS=1-5 TYPE=RADIUS MASS
```

**Custom Weights**:
```plumed
w: CONSTANT VALUES=1,2,2,3,4
g: GYRATION ATOMS=1-5 TYPE=RADIUS WEIGHTS=w
PRINT ARG=g FILE=colvar
```

**Tensor Properties**: You can also compute the trace of the gyration tensor:
```plumed
w: CONSTANT VALUES=1,2,2,3,4
g: GYRATION ATOMS=1-5 TYPE=TRACE WEIGHTS=w
PRINT ARG=g FILE=colvar
```

**Advanced Application**: Calculate radius of gyration for the largest cluster in a contact map:
```plumed
c1: CONTACT_MATRIX GROUP=1-100 SWITCH={RATIONAL R_0=0.1 D_MAX=0.5}
dfs: DFSCLUSTERING ARG=c1
w: CLUSTER_WEIGHTS CLUSTERS=dfs CLUSTER=1
g: GYRATION ATOMS=1-100 WEIGHTS=w TYPE=RADIUS
```

Sources: [Gyration.cpp](src/colvar/Gyration.cpp#L29-L100)

## Structural Comparison CVs

### RMSD

The `RMSD` (Root-Mean-Square Deviation) CV measures structural similarity between the current configuration and a reference structure, essential for studying folding, conformational transitions, and structural stability.

**Mathematical Concept**:
$$d(X,X') = \vert X-X' \vert$$

Where $X$ is the instantaneous atomic positions and $X'$ is the reference structure.

**Two Alignment Methods**:

1. **Simple Alignment** (`TYPE=SIMPLE`): Aligns geometric centers
$$d(X,X') = \sqrt{ \sum_i \sum_\alpha^{x,y,z}  \frac{w_i}{\sum_j w_j} ( X _{i,\alpha}-com _\alpha(X)-{X'} _{i,\alpha}+com _\alpha(X') )^2 }$$

2. **Optimal Alignment** (`TYPE=OPTIMAL`): Performs rotational alignment using Kabsch algorithm

**Basic Usage**:
```plumed
rmsd0: RMSD TYPE=SIMPLE REFERENCE=test0.pdb
PRINT ARG=rmsd0 FILE=colvar
```

**Optimal Alignment**:
```plumed
rmsd0: RMSD TYPE=OPTIMAL REFERENCE=test0.pdb NOPBC
PRINT ARG=rmsd0 FILE=colvar
```

> [!TIP]
> Use `TYPE=OPTIMAL` for studying protein folding where internal motions matter more than overall translation/rotation. Use `TYPE=SIMPLE` when you want to include overall structural displacement.

**Multiple Reference Comparison**:
```plumed
rmsd0: RMSD TYPE=OPTIMAL REFERENCE=test0.pdb NOPBC
rmsd1: RMSD TYPE=OPTIMAL REFERENCE=test1.pdb NOPBC
rmsd2: RMSD TYPE=OPTIMAL REFERENCE=test2.pdb NOPBC
sum: COMBINE ARG=* PERIODIC=NO
RESTRAINT ARG=sum AT=20.0 KAPPA=1.0
```

This example combines deviations from multiple reference structures, which is useful for analyzing multi-state systems.

Sources: [RMSD.cpp](src/colvar/RMSD.cpp#L43-L100), [regtest rt0](regtest/basic/rt0/plumed.dat#L3-L18)

### POSITION

The `POSITION` CV extracts coordinate components of individual atoms or groups of atoms, useful for tracking specific particles or calculating custom geometric descriptors.

**Basic Usage**:
```plumed
p: POSITION ATOM=1
PRINT ARG=p.x,p.y,p.z FILE=colvar
```

**Multiple Atoms**:
```plumed
p: POSITION ATOMS=1-4
PRINT ARG=p.x,p.y,p.z FILE=colvar
```

**PBC Handling**:
- **Scaled Components** (recommended for PBC systems): Output coordinates in -0.5 to 0.5 domain
```plumed
p: POSITION ATOM=1 SCALED_COMPONENTS
PRINT ARG=p.a,p.b,p.c FILE=colvar
```

- **Absolute Position** (use with caution): Requires fixed reference frame
```plumed
# First align to template to fix reference frame
p: POSITION ATOM=1 NOPBC
PRINT ARG=p.x,p.y,p.z FILE=colvar
```

> [!TIP]
> Never use `NOPBC` with POSITION unless you have explicitly fixed the reference frame using `FIT_TO_TEMPLATE` and have position restraints or other absolute constraints in your system.

**WHOLEMOLECULES Option**: Ensures molecules are reassembled if broken by periodic boundaries:
```plumed
p: POSITION ATOMS=1-4 WHOLEMOLECULES
PRINT ARG=p.x,p.y,p.z FILE=colvar
```

Sources: [Position.cpp](src/colvar/Position.cpp#L34-L100)

## Common Features Across Basic CVs

All basic collective variables share several important features:

### Periodic Boundary Condition Handling

| CV | Default Behavior | NOPBC Flag Available |
|----|------------------|---------------------|
| DISTANCE | Accounts for PBC | Yes |
| ANGLE | Handles broken molecules | Yes |
| TORSION | Handles broken molecules | Yes |
| COORDINATION | PBC-aware | Yes |
| GYRATION | PBC-aware | Yes |
| RMSD | Optional | Yes |
| POSITION | Scaled components | Yes |

### Atom Selection Syntax

PLUMED provides flexible atom selection methods:

```plumed
# Single atom
ATOM=1

# Range
ATOMS=1-10

# Multiple atoms
ATOMS=1,5,10,15

# Using GROUP definitions
g: GROUP ATOMS=1-100
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=g,50

# Using index files (GROMACS format)
g: GROUP NDX_FILE=groups.ndx NDX_GROUP=Protein
```

### Neighbor List Optimization

For CVs involving many pairwise calculations (like COORDINATION), neighbor lists dramatically improve performance:

```plumed
COORDINATION GROUPA=1-1000 GROUPB=2001-3000 R_0=0.3 
  NLIST NL_CUTOFF=0.5 NL_STRIDE=100
```

The neighbor list is updated every 100 steps and includes all atoms within 0.5 nm, ensuring all contacts within 0.3 nm are correctly identified.

Sources: [Coordination.cpp](src/colvar/Coordination.cpp#L52-L56)

## Practical Workflow Guide

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Define Atoms] --> B[Choose CV Type]
    B --> C{CV Category?}
    
    C -->|Distance| D[DISTANCE/ANGLE/TORSION]
    C -->|Coordination| E[COORDINATION]
    C -->|Geometry| F[GYRATION/RMSD]
    C -->|Position| G[POSITION]
    
    D --> H[Configure PBC Handling]
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    
    H --> I[Set Parameters]
    I --> J[Add Neighbor List<br>if many pairs]
    J --> K[Output with PRINT]
```

## Best Practices for Beginners

1. **Start Simple**: Begin with a single CV (e.g., DISTANCE or ANGLE) to understand the system's behavior before adding complexity.

2. **Visualize First**: Use `PRINT` with high frequency to output CV values and plot them to understand the dynamics before adding bias.

3. **Check Periodicity**: Always verify whether your CV should be periodic. Most distance-based CVs should handle PBCs automatically.

4. **Test Derivatives**: Use regression test patterns to verify CV derivatives:
```plumed
d: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2
dn: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2 NUMERICAL_DERIVATIVES
DUMPDERIVATIVES ARG={d dn} FILE=check
```

5. **Use Groups**: Define atom groups with the `GROUP` action for cleaner, more maintainable input files.

Sources: [regtest rt1](regtest/basic/rt1/plumed.dat#L9-L16), [regtest rt2](regtest/basic/rt2/plumed.dat#L1-L9)

- Learn about **[Metadynamics Fundamentals](4-metadynamics-fundamentals)** to understand how to bias these CVs and explore free energy landscapes
- Explore **[CV Fundamentals and Common CVs](10-cv-fundamentals-and-common-cvs)** for deeper insights into CV theory and advanced implementations
- Study the **[Action Framework and Execution Model](6-action-framework-and-execution-model)** to understand how PLUMED processes CV calculations
- Review **[Path-Based Collective Variables](11-path-based-collective-variables)** for techniques like PATHMSD that track progress along reaction coordinates
- Discover **[Multi-Component CVs](12-multi-component-cvs)** for working with groups of similar CVs simultaneously

By mastering these basic collective variables, you've built the foundation for implementing sophisticated enhanced sampling techniques and analyzing complex molecular systems.

# Metadynamics Fundamentals



This page introduces the core concepts and implementation details of metadynamics in PLUMED. Metadynamics is an enhanced sampling method that adds a history-dependent bias potential to drive exploration of collective variable (CV) space and reconstruct free energy surfaces.

## Mathematical Foundation

Metadynamics builds a bias potential by depositing Gaussian functions at regular intervals along the trajectory in CV space. The bias potential at time t is expressed as:

$$
V(\vec{s},t) = \sum_{k\tau < t} W(k\tau) \exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{d} \frac{(s_i - s_i^{(0)}(k\tau))^2}{2\sigma_i^2}\right)
$$

where $s_i$ are the collective variables, $W(k\tau)$ is the height of the Gaussian deposited at step $k\tau$, and $\sigma_i$ defines the Gaussian width for each CV. This history-dependent potential forces the system away from kinetic traps by filling free energy minima with successive Gaussian deposits, eventually allowing the system to explore unvisited regions of the energy landscape [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L26-L34).

The key theoretical insight is that the time-averaged bias potential converges to the negative free energy surface:

$$
V(\vec{s}) = -F(\vec{s})
$$

This relationship enables free energy reconstruction from the accumulated bias potential, which can be analyzed during post-processing using the `sum_hills` utility [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L35-L38).

## Architecture Overview

The metadynamics implementation in PLUMED follows a modular architecture where the `MetaD` class inherits from the base `Bias` class, which itself integrates multiple action interfaces. This design provides a clear separation between the bias calculation logic and the action execution framework.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ActionPilot {
        <<Action>>
        +update()
    }
    
    class ActionWithValue {
        <<Action>>
        +set()
        +get()
        +addDerivative()
    }
    
    class ActionWithArguments {
        <<Action>>
        +getArgument()
        +getNumberOfArguments()
    }
    
    class Bias {
        <<Abstract Base>>
        -std::vector~double~ outputForces
        -Value* valueBias
        +setOutputForce(int, double)
        +setBias(double)
        +apply()
    }
    
    class MetaD {
        -double height0_
        -double stride_
        -bool welltemp_
        -double biasf_
        -bool grid_
        -std::unique_ptr~Grid~ BiasGrid_
        +calculate()
        +update()
        +getBias()
        +getHeight()
    }
    
    class Gaussian {
        +double height
        +std::vector~double~ center
        +std::vector~double~ sigma
        +bool multivariate
    }
    
    class Grid {
        +getValue()
        +addValueAndDerivatives()
        +getNeighbors()
    }
    
    ActionPilot <|-- ActionWithArguments
    ActionWithValue <|-- ActionWithArguments
    ActionWithArguments <|-- Bias
    Bias <|-- MetaD
    MetaD --> Gaussian : stores
    MetaD --> Grid : uses
```

The bias framework provides essential functionality through the `Bias` base class, including force output management via `setOutputForce()` and bias value setting through `setBias()` [Bias.h](/src/bias/Bias.h#L66-L77). This allows metadynamics to seamlessly integrate with PLUMED's action execution model while providing specialized functionality for hill deposition and free energy reconstruction.

## Standard Metadynamics Configuration

### Basic Parameters

The minimal configuration for standard metadynamics requires specifying the collective variables to bias, Gaussian widths, initial hill height, and deposition frequency. Here is a typical two-dimensional example:

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,5
d2: DISTANCE ATOMS=2,4
restraint: METAD ARG=d1,d2 SIGMA=0.2,0.2 HEIGHT=0.3 PACE=500
PRINT ARG=d1,d2,restraint.bias STRIDE=100 FILE=COLVAR
```

In this example, distances between atoms (3,5) and (2,4) serve as collective variables. Gaussian hills with height 0.3 kJ/mol and widths of 0.2 nm in each CV direction are added every 500 MD steps. The CV values and bias potential are recorded to the COLVAR file every 100 steps [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L45-L56).

### Configuration Parameters

| Parameter | Required | Description | Units |
|-----------|----------|-------------|-------|
| `ARG` | Yes | Collective variables to bias | CV-dependent |
| `SIGMA` | Yes | Gaussian width(s) for each CV | CV-dependent |
| `HEIGHT` | No | Initial Gaussian hill height | kJ/mol |
| `PACE` | Yes | Steps between hill depositions | dimensionless |
| `FILE` | No | Output file for hill information | filename |

The `SIGMA` parameter can be specified as a comma-separated list matching the number of CVs. Each value determines the standard deviation of the Gaussian in the corresponding CV dimension [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L750-L767).

## Grid-Based Bias Evaluation

### Performance Optimization

In basic implementations, computational cost scales linearly with simulation time as the number of deposited hills increases. PLUMED addresses this through grid-based bias storage, where the potential is discretized onto a multidimensional grid for efficient evaluation [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L60-L62).

Grid configuration requires defining boundaries and resolution:

```plumed
t1: TORSION ATOMS=1,2,3,4
t2: TORSION ATOMS=5,6,7,8
m: METAD ARG=t1,t2 SIGMA=0.1,0.1 HEIGHT=1.2 PACE=500 
    GRID_MIN=-pi,-pi GRID_MAX=pi,pi GRID_BIN=100,100
PRINT ARG=t1,t2,m.bias STRIDE=100 FILE=COLVAR
```

### Grid Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| `GRID_MIN` | Lower boundary for each CV dimension | None (required) |
| `GRID_MAX` | Upper boundary for each CV dimension | None (required) |
| `GRID_BIN` | Number of grid points per dimension | None (required) |
| `GRID_SPACING` | Grid spacing alternative to `GRID_BIN` | None |
| `GRID_SPARSE` | Use sparse grid representation | false |

PLUMED validates grid spacing against Gaussian width to prevent artifacts. The grid spacing should be less than half the Gaussian width: if this condition is violated, a warning is issued [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L1384-L1396).

### Hill Evaluation on Grids

When a new Gaussian is deposited, PLUMED calculates its support region—points on the grid where the Gaussian contribution is above the cutoff threshold (typically 10^-8 of the peak). Only points within this support region are updated, providing significant computational savings:

```cpp
std::vector<unsigned> nneighb = getGaussianSupport(hill);
std::vector<Grid::index_t> neighbors = BiasGrid_->getNeighbors(hill.center, nneighb);
// Update only neighbor grid points
for(size_t i = 0; i < neighbors.size(); ++i) {
    BiasGrid_->addValueAndDerivatives(ineigh, bias, der);
}
```

This approach maintains O(1) complexity for bias evaluation regardless of the total number of deposited hills [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L1762-L1795).

> [!TIP]
> Grid storage is essential for long simulations. Without grids, the computational cost increases linearly with the number of deposited hills, making simulations with more than 10,000-100,000 hills prohibitively expensive.

## Well-Tempered Metadynamics

### Enhanced Convergence

Well-tempered metadynamics modifies the standard algorithm by reducing hill heights as the bias grows, ensuring convergence to a finite free energy estimate. The hill height at step t is scaled according to:

$$
W(t) = W_0 \exp\left(-\frac{V(\vec{s},t)}{k_B T (\gamma - 1)}\right)
$$

where $\gamma$ is the bias factor (typically 10-100), $W_0$ is the initial height, and $V(\vec{s},t)$ is the current bias potential [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L2230-L2238).

### Configuration

Well-tempered metadynamics is activated by specifying both `BIASFACTOR` and `TEMP`:

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,5
d2: DISTANCE ATOMS=2,4
restraint: METAD ARG=d1,d2 SIGMA=0.2,0.2 HEIGHT=0.3 BIASFACTOR=10 PACE=500
PRINT ARG=d1,d2,restraint.bias STRIDE=100 FILE=COLVAR
```

The bias factor $\gamma$ controls the exploration depth. A value of 10 provides moderate exploration while maintaining good convergence properties [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L196-L204).

### Well-Tempered Parameters

| Parameter | Required | Description | Typical Values |
|-----------|----------|-------------|----------------|
| `BIASFACTOR` | Yes | Bias factor $\gamma$ | 5-100 |
| `TEMP` | Conditional | Simulation temperature (in K) | from MD engine or specified |

> [!TIP]
> The hills file in well-tempered metadynamics stores rescaled heights corresponding to $-F(\vec{s})$ rather than the actual bias potential. This enables restarting simulations with different bias factors while maintaining the correct free energy estimate.

## Advanced Variants

### Adaptive Gaussian Widths

PLUMED supports adaptive Gaussian schemes that adjust hill widths based on system dynamics, useful when CVs have different sensitivities or cover varying scales:

- **Diffusion-based (`ADAPTIVE=DIFF`)**: Width adapts to the CV space covered during a specified number of time steps
- **Geometry-based (`ADAPTIVE=GEOM`)**: Width adapts to the Cartesian space covered by CV variations

Diffusion example:

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,5
d2: DISTANCE ATOMS=2,4
restraint: METAD ARG=d1,d2 SIGMA=20 HEIGHT=0.3 PACE=500 ADAPTIVE=DIFF
```

Geometry example:

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,5
d2: DISTANCE ATOMS=2,4
restraint: METAD ARG=d1,d2 SIGMA=0.05 HEIGHT=0.3 PACE=500 ADAPTIVE=GEOM
```

Width limits can be controlled with `SIGMA_MIN` and `SIGMA_MAX` [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L238-L290).

### Multiple Walkers Metadynamics

Multiple walkers enable parallel exploration of CV space by synchronizing bias between multiple replicas:

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,5
restraint: METAD ...
   ARG=d1 SIGMA=0.05 HEIGHT=0.3 PACE=500
   WALKERS_N=10
   WALKERS_ID=3
   WALKERS_DIR=../
   WALKERS_RSTRIDE=100
...
```

Parameters:
- `WALKERS_N`: Total number of walkers
- `WALKERS_ID`: Current walker's ID (0 to N-1)
- `WALKERS_DIR`: Directory containing other walkers' hills files
- `WALKERS_RSTRIDE`: Frequency of reading other walkers' data [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L307-L320)

### Acceleration Factor Calculation

Infrequent metadynamics analyzes transition kinetics using the acceleration factor, which quantifies rate enhancement:

```plumed
psi: ANGLE ATOMS=7,9,15
md1: METAD ...
 ARG=psi SIGMA=0.20
 HEIGHT=1.20 TEMP=300.0 BIASFACTOR=10
 PACE=500 GRID_MIN=0 GRID_MAX=pi GRID_BIN=10
 ACCELERATION
...
PRINT ARG=psi,md1.bias,md1.acc FILE=colvar STRIDE=10
```

The acceleration factor $\alpha(t)$ is computed as the time-average of $\exp(V(s,t)/k_B T)$ and accumulated continuously during the simulation [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L343-L353).

## Hill Storage and Restart

### Hills File Format

PLUMED records deposited Gaussians in the HILLS file (customizable with `FILE` parameter). Each entry contains:

- Time: Step number
- CV coordinates: Center of deposited Gaussian
- Sigma parameters: Gaussian widths
- Height: Gaussian amplitude (rescaled for well-tempered)
- biasf: Bias factor used [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L1828-L1879)

### Restart Procedure

Metadynamics simulations can be restarted using previously deposited hills:

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,5
d2: DISTANCE ATOMS=2,4
restraint: METAD ARG=d1,d2 SIGMA=0.2,0.2 HEIGHT=0.3 PACE=500 RESTART=YES
```

The `RESTART` flag causes PLUMED to read the existing HILLS file and reconstruct the bias potential from all previously deposited Gaussians [MetaD.cpp](/src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L1690-L1710).

## Summary

Metadynamics in PLUMED provides a flexible framework for enhanced sampling with the following key features:

- **Standard and well-tempered variants** with configurable hill deposition parameters
- **Grid-based storage** for computational efficiency in long simulations
- **Multiple advanced variants** including adaptive Gaussians, multiple walkers, and kinetic analysis
- **Robust restart capabilities** through hill file persistence
- **Free energy reconstruction** via post-processing with `sum_hills`

The implementation balances theoretical rigor with computational efficiency, making it suitable for studying complex free energy landscapes in molecular systems.

## Next Steps

After mastering these fundamentals, explore:

- [CV Fundamentals and Common CVs](10-cv-fundamentals-and-common-cvs) for building effective collective variables
- [Metadynamics Variants](14-metadynamics-variants) for specialized techniques including bias-exchange metadynamics
- [Reweighting and Free Energy Analysis](16-reweighting-and-free-energy-analysis) for analyzing biased simulations
- [Action Framework and Execution Model](6-action-framework-and-execution-model) for understanding the underlying architecture


# Umbrella Sampling and WHAM



This guide provides a comprehensive introduction to umbrella sampling and the Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM) as implemented in PLUMED2. These techniques enable the calculation of free energy surfaces along collective variables by combining data from multiple biased simulations, making them essential tools for studying rare events and conformational transitions in molecular dynamics simulations.

Sources: [src/wham/module.md](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/module.md#L1-L5), [src/wham/module.yml](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/module.yml#L1-L5)

## Theoretical Foundation

### Umbrella Sampling Overview

Umbrella sampling is a molecular dynamics technique that enhances sampling along specific reaction coordinates or collective variables by applying harmonic restraints. The method divides the free energy landscape into overlapping windows, each biased toward a different reference point along the collective variable. By running independent simulations in each window and subsequently reweighting the data, you can reconstruct the unbiased free energy profile across the entire range of interest.

The bias potential applied in each window follows a harmonic form: V_bias(ξ) = (κ/2)(ξ - ξ₀)², where κ is the force constant, ξ is the collective variable value, and ξ₀ is the reference position for that window. The key insight is that while each simulation samples only a restricted region, the overlapping regions between windows provide the information needed to stitch together the complete free energy surface.

Sources: [src/bias/Restraint.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/bias/Restraint.cpp#L1-L80)

### WHAM Mathematical Framework

The Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM) provides the formalism for combining data from multiple biased simulations. PLUMED2 implements the **binless formulation** of WHAM, which operates directly on individual configurations rather than requiring histogram binning.

The fundamental probability equation that WHAM maximizes is:

P(T) ∝ ∏_{j=1}^M ∏_{k=1}^N (c_k w_{kj} p_j)^{t_{kj}}

where the outer product runs over N trajectories with different biases, the inner product runs over M histogram bins, p_j is the unbiased probability we seek to extract, t_{kj} measures the number of frames from trajectory k in bin j, and w_{kj} is the weight factor accounting for the bias:

w_{kj} = e^{+βV_k(x_j)}

The normalization constants c_k ensure each biased probability distribution is normalized: ∑_j c_k w_{kj} p_j = 1. By maximizing the log-likelihood with Lagrange multipliers for the normalization constraints, we derive the iterative WHAM equations:

p_j ∝ (∑_{k=1}^N t_{kj})/(∑_k c_k w_{kj})
c_k = 1/(∑_{j=1}^M w_{kj} p_j)

Sources: [src/wham/Wham.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/Wham.cpp#L30-L95)

## PLUMED2 Architecture

### Component Overview

The WHAM implementation in PLUMED2 consists of three main components that work together to enable umbrella sampling analysis:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph MD_Simulations["MD Simulations"]
        R1[Replica 1<br/>ξ₀ = -3.00]
        R2[Replica 2<br/>ξ₀ = -1.45]
        R3[Replica 3<br/>ξ₀ = 0.10]
        R4[Replica 4<br/>ξ₀ = 1.65]
    end
    
    subgraph PLUMED_Actions["PLUMED2 Actions"]
        RESTRAINT[RESTRAINT<br/>Applies harmonic bias]
        GATHER[GATHER_REPLICAS<br/>Collects bias values]
        CONCAT[CONCATENATE<br/>Merges replicas]
        COLLECT[COLLECT<br/>Time series collection]
        WHAM[WHAM<br/>Computes weights]
        DUMP[DUMPVECTOR/DUMPGRID<br/>Output results]
    end
    
    subgraph Analysis["Analysis & Output"]
        WEIGHTS[Configuration weights]
        HIST[WHAM_HISTOGRAM<br/>Free energy histogram]
        FES[Free energy surface]
    end
    
    R1 -->|bias values| GATHER
    R2 -->|bias values| GATHER
    R3 -->|bias values| GATHER
    R4 -->|bias values| GATHER
    
    GATHER --> CONCAT
    CONCAT --> COLLECT
    COLLECT --> WHAM
    WHAM --> WEIGHTS
    WHAM --> HIST
    HIST --> FES
    WEIGHTS --> DUMP
    FES --> DUMP
    
    RESTRAINT -.->|Creates bias| R1
    RESTRAINT -.->|Creates bias| R2
    RESTRAINT -.->|Creates bias| R3
    RESTRAINT -.->|Creates bias| R4
```

Sources: [src/wham/WhamWeights.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/WhamWeights.cpp#L29-L65), [regtest/wham/rt-wham/plumed.dat](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/regtest/wham/rt-wham/plumed.dat#L1-L29)

### WHAM Core Implementation

The `WHAM` action implements the iterative solution to the WHAM equations. Key implementation details include:

**Initialization**: The action reads temperature, maximum iterations, and convergence tolerance from input parameters. Temperature can be obtained from the MD engine or explicitly specified.

**Bias Processing**: For each configuration, the algorithm computes the exponential weight factor: exp[(-V_bias + V_min)/kT], where V_min prevents numerical overflow by normalizing to the minimum bias value.

**Iterative Solution**: The algorithm alternates between:
1. Computing final weights for each configuration: w_j = 1/∑_k (exp_{jk}/Z_k)
2. Recomputing partition functions: Z_k = ∑_j (w_j × exp_{jk})
3. Checking convergence based on changes in Z values

The binless formulation's key advantage is that only ∑_k t_{kj} (total configurations in each bin) enters the final equations, eliminating the need to track which replica generated each frame.

Sources: [src/wham/Wham.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/Wham.cpp#L97-L233)

### Shortcut Action Architecture

The `WHAM_WEIGHTS` action provides a convenient shortcut that automatically orchestrates the full WHAM workflow. This action internally generates the necessary pipeline:

| Internal Action | Purpose |
|----------------|---------|
| GATHER_REPLICAS | Collects bias values from all replicas |
| CONCATENATE | Merges replica data into single vector |
| COLLECT | Creates time series of bias values |
| WHAM | Performs the WHAM weight calculation |
| DUMPVECTOR | Outputs final weights to file |

This abstraction simplifies user input while maintaining flexibility for advanced users who need custom configurations.

Sources: [src/wham/WhamWeights.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/WhamWeights.cpp#L68-L118)

## Practical Implementation

### Basic Umbrella Sampling Workflow

The complete workflow for umbrella sampling with WHAM analysis involves three stages:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Stage1["Stage 1: Biased Simulations"]
        A1[Define collective variables]
        A2[Configure RESTRAINT<br/>for each window]
        A3[Run independent simulations<br/>for each window]
    end
    
    subgraph Stage2["Stage 2: Data Preparation"]
        B1[Concatenate trajectories<br/>from all windows]
        B2[Prepare PLUMED input<br/>for analysis]
    end
    
    subgraph Stage3["Stage 3: WHAM Analysis"]
        C1[Run PLUMED driver<br/>with MPI]
        C2[Compute WHAM weights]
        C3[Generate free energy surface]
        C4[Analyze results]
    end
    
    Stage1 --> Stage2
    Stage2 --> Stage3
```

### Configuration Options

The WHAM implementation provides several tunable parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| MAXITER | 1000 | Maximum number of WHAM iterations |
| WHAMTOL | 1×10⁻¹⁰ | Convergence threshold for partition function changes |
| TEMP | From MD engine | Simulation temperature (required if not passed by MD) |
| STRIDE | 1 | Frequency of bias storage for WHAM calculation |

The convergence criterion is based on the sum of squared logarithmic changes in the partition functions across all replicas: ∑_k [log(Z_k/Z_k^old)]² < WHAMTOL.

Sources: [src/wham/Wham.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/Wham.cpp#L117-L129)

### Complete Example

The following example demonstrates a complete umbrella sampling analysis on a dihedral angle using four windows:

```plumed
# Define collective variables
phi: TORSION ATOMS=5,7,9,15
psi: TORSION ATOMS=7,9,15,17

# Apply harmonic restraints at different reference values
rp: RESTRAINT ARG=phi KAPPA=50.0 AT=@replicas:{-3.00,-1.45,0.10,1.65}

# Compute WHAM weights for reweighting
WHAM_WEIGHTS BIAS=rp.bias TEMP=300 FILE=wham-weights
```

This input must be executed with MPI to handle multiple replicas:

```bash
mpirun -np 4 plumed driver --mf_xtc alltraj.xtc --multi 4
```

For free energy reconstruction, you can also use the histogram-based approach:

```plumed
hh: WHAM_HISTOGRAM ARG=phi BIAS=rp.bias TEMP=300 GRID_MIN=-pi GRID_MAX=pi GRID_BIN=50
fes: CONVERT_TO_FES ARG=hh TEMP=300
DUMPGRID ARG=fes STRIDE=0 FILE=fes.dat
```

Sources: [regtest/wham/rt-wham/plumed.dat](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/regtest/wham/rt-wham/plumed.dat#L1-L29)

### Input Parameter Comparison

The table below compares the two main approaches for WHAM analysis in PLUMED2:

| Feature | WHAM_WEIGHTS | WHAM + WHAM_HISTOGRAM |
|---------|--------------|----------------------|
| **Output** | Per-configuration weights | Histogram and free energy surface |
| **Use Case** | Reweighting observables | Direct free energy visualization |
| **Flexibility** | High (weights can be reused) | Medium (specific to CV grid) |
| **Complexity** | Low (single command) | Medium (multiple actions) |
| **Memory Usage** | Proportional to trajectory | Proportional to histogram bins |

> [!TIP]
> When working with large systems or long trajectories, consider using `STRIDE > 1` in `WHAM_WEIGHTS` to reduce memory usage. The WHAM algorithm is robust to subsampling as long as the stride is small compared to the correlation time of the system.

Sources: [src/wham/WhamWeights.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/WhamWeights.cpp#L29-L65)

## Advanced Considerations

### Binless vs. Binned WHAM

PLUMED2's binless WHAM implementation offers several advantages over traditional histogram-based methods:

1. **No binning artifacts**: Eliminates sensitivity to bin size selection
2. **Continuous resolution**: Preserves full trajectory resolution
3. **Memory efficiency**: No need to store large histograms
4. **Flexibility**: Weights can be applied to any observable calculation

The key innovation is recognizing that only the total count of configurations in each region (∑_k t_{kj}) matters, not which specific replica contributed them. This enables the algorithm to work with concatenated trajectories without replica tagging.

Sources: [src/wham/Wham.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/Wham.cpp#L64-L95)

### Convergence and Performance

The WHAM iteration typically converges in 10-100 iterations for well-behaved systems. Factors affecting convergence include:

- **Window overlap**: Insufficient overlap between windows slows convergence
- **Force constant**: Very stiff restraints (high κ) reduce sampling efficiency
- **Temperature**: Lower temperatures require more iterations due to exponential terms
- **Number of replicas**: More replicas increase computational cost per iteration

For production calculations, monitor the convergence behavior and adjust `MAXITER` and `WHAMTOL` accordingly. The default values are conservative for most applications.

> [!TIP]
> The minimum bias subtraction in the exponential calculation (using V_min) is crucial for numerical stability. Always ensure your bias values are finite and well-defined before WHAM analysis.

Sources: [src/wham/Wham.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/wham/Wham.cpp#L152-L167)

### Integration with Collective Variables

The WHAM framework integrates seamlessly with PLUMED2's extensive collective variable library. Any CV that produces a scalar value can be used with umbrella sampling and WHAM:

- **Distance-based CVs**: DISTANCE, ANGLE, TORSION
- **Path CVs**: PATH, PATHMSD
- **Coordination CVs**: COORDINATION, Q4, Q6
- **Custom CVs**: User-defined CVs through the plugin interface

The RESTRAINT action supports both scalar and vector arguments, enabling multi-dimensional umbrella sampling along multiple CVs simultaneously.

Sources: [src/bias/Restraint.cpp](/plumed/plumed2/blob/master/src/bias/Restraint.cpp#L40-L65)

## Next Steps

To deepen your understanding of PLUMED2's capabilities, consider exploring these related topics:

- **[Collective Variables Fundamentals](10-cv-fundamentals-and-common-cvs)**: Learn about the full range of available CVs and their implementation
- **[Restraints and Walls](15-restraints-and-walls)**: Explore other biasing methods including upper/lower walls and moving restraints
- **[Reweighting and Free Energy Analysis](16-reweighting-and-free-energy-analysis)**: Discover alternative reweighting techniques including metadynamics reweighting
