# Creating New Bias Methods



This page provides a comprehensive guide for advanced developers seeking to implement new biasing potentials in PLUMED. Bias methods are the computational engines behind enhanced sampling algorithms, enabling exploration of rare events and free energy landscape reconstruction. This documentation covers the architectural foundations, implementation patterns, and practical considerations for creating production-ready bias components.

## Bias Architecture Overview

The PLUMED bias system employs a **multiple inheritance architecture** that combines three critical base classes, each responsible for distinct aspects of bias functionality. This design promotes code reuse and enforces a consistent interface across all bias implementations.
Sources: [src/bias/Bias.h](src/bias/Bias.h#L30-L50)

### Core Inheritance Structure

Every bias method inherits from three base classes that collectively provide:

- **ActionPilot**: Manages execution timing through the STRIDE parameter, enabling multiple time stepping for computational efficiency. This allows biases to be applied less frequently than every MD step when appropriate.
Sources: [src/core/ActionPilot.h](src/core/ActionPilot.h#L20-L30)

- **ActionWithValue**: Provides infrastructure for storing scalar or vector output values with optional derivative support. This is essential for bias potentials that compute both the energy and forces (∂V/∂CV).
Sources: [src/core/ActionWithValue.h](src/core/ActionWithValue.h#L30-L60)

- **ActionWithArguments**: Handles input collective variable dependencies, enabling biases to operate on previously computed CVs. This facilitates the composition of complex biasing hierarchies.
Sources: [src/core/ActionWithArguments.h](src/core/ActionWithArguments.h#L30-L50)

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Action {
        <<abstract>>
        +"registerKeywords()"
        +"calculate()"
        +"apply()"
    }
    
    class ActionPilot {
        +"onStep()"
        +"getStride()"
        -actionStride
    }
    
    class ActionWithValue {
        +"addValue()"
        +"addComponentWithDerivatives()"
        +"setValue()"
        +"getPntrToValue()"
        -values
    }
    
    class ActionWithArguments {
        +"getArgument()"
        +"getPntrToArgument()"
        +"getNumberOfArguments()"
        +"parseArgumentList()"
        -arguments
    }
    
    class Bias {
        +"setOutputForce()"
        +"setBias()"
        +"getNumberOfDerivatives()"
        -outputForces
        -valueBias
    }
    
    Bias --> ActionPilot
    Bias --> ActionWithValue
    Bias --> ActionWithArguments
    ActionPilot --> Action
    ActionWithValue --> Action
    ActionWithArguments --> Action
```

### Bias Lifecycle

The execution model for biases follows a well-defined sequence integrated into the MD timestep:

1. **Registration Phase**: During initialization, biases register their keywords and requirements through the ActionRegister mechanism.
Sources: [src/core/ActionRegister.h](src/core/ActionRegister.h#L30-L50)

2. **Calculation Phase**: On active timesteps (determined by STRIDE), the `calculate()` method computes the bias potential and forces. The base Bias class automatically handles derivative accumulation and force scaling.
Sources: [src/bias/Bias.cpp](src/bias/Bias.cpp#L50-L80)

3. **Application Phase**: The `apply()` method propagates forces to the underlying collective variables, with automatic scaling when STRIDE > 1 to preserve proper time averaging.
Sources: [src/bias/Bias.cpp](src/bias/Bias.cpp#L50-L110)

## Implementation Framework

Creating a new bias method requires implementing a specific interface and following established conventions. The implementation template below demonstrates the minimal required components.

### File Structure and Basic Template

Bias implementations reside in `src/bias/` as single `.cpp` files. Each file must include the registration macro and implement three core components:

```cpp
#include "Bias.h"
#include "core/ActionRegister.h"

namespace PLMD {
namespace bias {

//+PLUMEDOC BIAS MYBIAS
/*
Documentation string describing your bias method. Include mathematical formulation,
explanation of parameters, and practical usage examples.
*/
//+ENDPLUMEDOC

class MyBias : public Bias {
  // Member variables to store parameters and state
public:
  explicit MyBias(const ActionOptions&);
  void calculate() override;
  static void registerKeywords(Keywords& keys);
};

PLUMED_REGISTER_ACTION(MyBias,"MYBIAS")
```

### Constructor Implementation

The constructor serves three critical purposes: parameter parsing, state initialization, and component registration.
Sources: [src/bias/Restraint.cpp](src/bias/Restraint.cpp#L60-L90)

```cpp
MyBias::MyBias(const ActionOptions& ao):
  PLUMED_BIAS_INIT(ao),
  // Initialize member variables
  parameter1(getNumberOfArguments()),
  parameter2(getNumberOfArguments(),0.0) {
  
  // Parse input keywords
  parseVector("PARAMETER1",parameter1);
  parseVector("PARAMETER2",parameter2);
  checkRead();  // Ensure all input was consumed
  
  // Log parsed values for verification
  log.printf("  parameter1 values:");
  for(unsigned i=0; i<parameter1.size(); i++) {
    log.printf(" %f",parameter1[i]);
  }
  log.printf("\n");
  
  // Add optional output components
  addComponent("force2");
  componentIsNotPeriodic("force2");
  valueForce2 = getPntrToComponent("force2");
}
```

> [!TIP]
> Always use `checkRead()` after parsing to catch typos and undefined parameters early in the development cycle. This prevents silent failures where critical parameters are silently ignored.

### Keyword Registration

The `registerKeywords` method defines all input parameters and documentation strings. Inheritance from Bias automatically registers standard keywords like ARG and STRIDE.
Sources: [src/bias/Bias.cpp](src/bias/Bias.cpp#L38-L48)

```cpp
void MyBias::registerKeywords(Keywords& keys) {
  Bias::registerKeywords(keys);
  
  // Define compulsory parameters
  keys.add("compulsory","PARAMETER1","description of required parameter");
  
  // Define optional parameters with defaults
  keys.add("optional","PARAMETER2","0.0","description of optional parameter");
  
  // Define output components
  keys.addOutputComponent("force2","default","scalar","description of force squared output");
}
```

### Calculate Method

The `calculate()` method implements the core physics: computing the bias potential and forces. This is called every active timestep.
Sources: [src/bias/Restraint.cpp](src/bias/Restraint.cpp#L110-L146)

```cpp
void MyBias::calculate() {
  double energy = 0.0;
  
  // Loop over all collective variables (arguments)
  for(unsigned i=0; i<getNumberOfArguments(); ++i) {
    // Get current CV value with proper periodicity handling
    const double cv = difference(i, target[i], getArgument(i));
    
    // Compute force: F = -∂V/∂CV
    const double force = -computeForce(cv, parameter1[i], parameter2[i]);
    
    // Accumulate energy contribution
    energy += computeEnergy(cv, parameter1[i], parameter2[i]);
    
    // Set force on CV (automatically sets derivative = -force)
    setOutputForce(i, force);
  }
  
  // Set the bias potential value
  setBias(energy);
  
  // Update optional output components
  valueForce2->set(computeForceSquared());
}
```

## Implementation Patterns by Complexity

Different bias implementations require varying levels of complexity. Understanding these patterns helps select the appropriate architecture for your use case.

### Simple Time-Independent Biases

The **Restraint** class exemplifies simple harmonic and linear restraints. These biases maintain no internal state between timesteps and compute forces based solely on current CV values.
Sources: [src/bias/Restraint.cpp](src/bias/Restraint.cpp#L1-L146)

**Key characteristics**:
- Stateless calculation (no history dependence)
- Direct force computation from CV displacement
- Single output component (bias potential)

**Mathematical formulation**:
```
V(x) = Σᵢ [κᵢ/2 × (xᵢ - aᵢ)² + mᵢ × (xᵢ - aᵢ)]
Fᵢ = -∂V/∂xᵢ = -[κᵢ × (xᵢ - aᵢ) + mᵢ]
```

### History-Dependent Biases

The **ABMD** (Adaptive Biasing Molecular Dynamics) class demonstrates moderate complexity with time-dependent bias minima. This method implements a ratchet-like potential that evolves based on CV history.
Sources: [src/bias/ABMD.cpp](src/bias/ABMD.cpp#L40-L100)

**State management requirements**:
- Store historical minimum values: `std::vector<double> min`
- Track random number generators for noise: `std::vector<Random> random`
- Update state each timestep based on current CV values

**Complexity considerations**:
- Need persistent state between calculate() calls
- Potential dependency on step count or simulation time
- May require file I/O for restart capabilities

### Complex History-Dependent Biases

**Metadynamics** represents the most complex bias type, requiring Gaussian kernel accumulation, grid storage/lookup, and extensive file I/O. The implementation spans over 2800 lines.
Sources: [src/bias/MetaD.cpp](src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L1-L2809)

**Advanced features**:
- Multiple kernel storage strategies (direct evaluation, neighbor lists, grids)
- Hill file I/O for restart capability
- Well-Tempered Metadynamics with adaptive height scaling
- Parallel communication for MPI runs

> [!TIP]
> For complex biases, consider separating concerns into private helper methods. The MetaD implementation uses numerous private methods for initialization, hill management, and grid operations to maintain code readability.

### Pattern Comparison

| Pattern | State Required | File I/O | Typical LOC | Examples |
|---------|---------------|----------|-------------|----------|
| Time-independent | None | Rarely | 50-150 | RESTRAINT, WALLS |
| State-dependent | Internal state | Optional | 150-500 | ABMD, MovingRestraint |
| Complex | Grids, history | Essential | 500-2800+ | METAD, PBMetaD, MaxEnt |

## Force Application and Derivative Handling

The Bias base class provides automatic force application infrastructure that developers must understand to correctly implement bias methods.

### OutputForce Mechanism

The `setOutputForce(i, force)` method performs two critical operations: Sources: [src/bias/Bias.h](src/bias/Bias.h#L60-L70)

1. Stores the force in the internal `outputForces` vector
2. Automatically sets the derivative of the bias with respect to CV i to `-force`

This enforces the thermodynamic relationship: `Fᵢ = -∂V/∂xᵢ`

```cpp
inline void Bias::setOutputForce(int i, double force) {
  outputForces[i] = force;
  valueBias->addDerivative(i, -force);
}
```

### Multiple Time Stepping Considerations

When STRIDE > 1, forces are automatically scaled by the stride value to preserve proper time averaging. This enables computational efficiency without biasing the physics.
Sources: [src/bias/Bias.cpp](src/bias/Bias.cpp#L50-L65)

```cpp
void Bias::apply() {
  const unsigned noa = getNumberOfArguments();
  
  if(onStep()) {
    double gstr = static_cast<double>(getStride());
    for(unsigned i=0; i<noa; ++i) {
      // Force is scaled by stride
      getPntrToArgument(i)->addForce(gstr * outputForces[i]);
    }
  }
  // ... rest of application logic
}
```

The documentation for STRIDE usage emphasizes that this technique can significantly speed up simulations when biasing expensive CVs.
Sources: [src/bias/module.md](src/bias/module.md#L30-L55)

### Periodic Boundaries

When computing CV displacements, always use the `difference()` method instead of simple subtraction. This ensures proper handling of periodic CVs through the minimum image convention.
Sources: [src/bias/Restraint.cpp](src/bias/Restraint.cpp#L115-L120)

```cpp
// CORRECT: Handles periodicity properly
const double cv = difference(i, at[i], getArgument(i));

// INCORRECT: Fails for periodic CVs
const double cv = getArgument(i) - at[i];
```

## Registration and Integration

The PLUMED registration system automatically integrates new bias methods into the framework through compile-time registration.

### Action Registration Macro

The `PLUMED_REGISTER_ACTION` macro performs registration at program initialization: Sources: [src/core/ActionRegister.h](src/core/ActionRegister.h#L70-L80)

```cpp
PLUMED_REGISTER_ACTION(MyBias,"MYBIAS")
```

This macro expands to code that:
1. Creates a static object whose constructor runs before main()
2. Registers the class creator and keyword function in the global ActionRegister
3. Makes "MYBIAS" available as a keyword in PLUMED input files

### Documentation Integration

The `+PLUMEDOC` and `+ENDPLUMEDOC` markers define the documentation block that is automatically extracted for the user manual.
Sources: [developer-doc/AddingAColvar.md](developer-doc/AddingAColvar.md#L20-L40)

Best practices for bias documentation:
- Provide clear mathematical formulation using LaTeX
- Include at least one complete working example
- Explain physical interpretation of all parameters
- Reference relevant publications when applicable
- Document any known limitations or performance considerations

## Testing Strategy

Comprehensive testing is essential for bias method reliability. PLUMED provides a regression testing framework that should be leveraged for all new biases.
Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200)

### Regression Test Structure

Each regression test resides in `regtest/` with a specific naming convention: `rt-something`. The test directory must contain: Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L30-L60)

1. **config**: Configuration file specifying test parameters
2. **Makefile**: Standard makefile (usually copied from existing tests)
3. **plumed.dat**: PLUMED input file testing the bias
4. **Reference files**: `.reference` files for output verification

### Config File Example

```bash
type=driver
plumed_modules=bias
arg="--plumed plumed.dat --trajectory-stride 50 --timestep 0.005 --ixyz trajectory.xyz --dump-forces forces --dump-forces-fmt=%8.4f"
extra_files="../../trajectories/trajectory.xyz"
```

### Testing Force Derivatives

For biases with analytical derivatives, verify correctness by comparing with numerical derivatives: Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L120-L170)

```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2
bias: MYBIAS ARG=d1 PARAM1=1.0 PARAM2=2.0
bias_n: MYBIAS ARG=d1 PARAM1=1.0 PARAM2=2.0 NUMERICAL_DERIVATIVES

DUMPDERIVATIVES ARG=bias,bias_n FILE=derivatives FMT=%8.4f
```

**Verification approach**:
- Compare analytical derivatives (column 3) with numerical derivatives (column 4)
- Differences should be within numerical precision
- Store only analytical derivatives in reference files (numerical values vary across architectures)

### Test Execution

Run regression tests with:
```bash
cd regtest/your_test_directory
make
```

This executes the test and compares output against `.reference` files.
Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L80-L100)

## Common Patterns and Utilities

PLUMED provides numerous utility classes and patterns that simplify bias implementation.

### Grid Storage

For biases that require storing multidimensional potentials (like metadynamics), the Grid class provides efficient storage and interpolation.
Sources: [src/tools/Grid.h](src/tools/Grid.h#L1-L50)

```cpp
#include "tools/Grid.h"

// Create grid with specified boundaries and binning
Grid myGrid(grid_min, grid_max, grid_bin, true, true);

// Set value at grid point
myGrid.setValue(indices, value);

// Get value at arbitrary position with interpolation
double value = myGrid.getValueAndDerivatives(position, derivatives);
```

### Random Number Generation

The Random class provides cross-platform reproducible random numbers essential for stochastic bias methods.
Sources: [src/bias/ABMD.cpp](src/bias/ABMD.cpp#L85-L95)

```cpp
#include "tools/Random.h"

Random random(seed);

// Gaussian-distributed random number
double gaussian = random.Gaussian();

// Uniform random in [0,1)
double uniform = random.RandU01();
```

### File I/O

PLUMED provides OFile and IFile classes for formatted input/output:

```cpp
#include "tools/OFile.h"

OFile ofile;
ofile.link(*this);
ofile.open("output.dat");

// Write formatted output
ofile.printf("%f %f %f\n", x, y, z);
```

## Performance Optimization Strategies

Bias methods can significantly impact simulation performance, especially when operating on expensive CVs.

### Computational Efficiency

**Avoid redundant calculations**:
- Cache expensive operations in member variables
- Precompute constants in the constructor
- Use appropriate data structures (vectors vs. maps)

**Optimize CV evaluation**:
- Use STRIDE > 1 for very expensive CVs
- Consider neighbor lists for grid-based biases
- Minimize memory allocations in calculate()

### Memory Efficiency

For complex biases like metadynamics: Sources: [src/bias/MetaD.cpp](src/bias/MetaD.cpp#L80-L120)

- Choose appropriate grid spacing (default: σ/5)
- Use sparse storage when possible
- Consider multiple timesteps to reduce evaluation frequency

### Parallel Execution

For MPI-parallel simulations:
- Ensure proper synchronization of bias state
- Communicate necessary data across ranks
- Test with different numbers of MPI ranks

## Step-by-Step Implementation Workflow

Follow this systematic approach when implementing a new bias method:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Define Mathematical Model] --> B[Create Bias.cpp File]
    B --> C[Implement Constructor]
    C --> D[Implement registerKeywords]
    D --> E[Implement calculate Method]
    E --> F[Write PLUMED Documentation]
    F --> G[Create Regression Test]
    G --> H{Verify Derivatives}
    H -->|Pass| I[Commit to Repository]
    H -->|Fail| E
```

### Detailed Implementation Steps

1. **Mathematical formulation**: Precisely define the bias potential V(x) and force F(x) = -∇V(x). Consider periodicity, boundary conditions, and state requirements.

2. **File creation**: Copy the template structure from existing bias implementations. Ensure proper include files are present.

3. **Constructor**: Parse all input parameters, initialize member variables, and register any additional output components.

4. **Keyword registration**: Define all input parameters with appropriate defaults and documentation. Use appropriate flag types (compulsory, optional, hidden).

5. **Calculate method**: Implement the core physics. Loop over CVs, compute displacements using `difference()`, calculate forces with proper sign, and set bias value.

6. **Documentation**: Write comprehensive user documentation including mathematical background, parameter descriptions, and working examples.

7. **Testing**: Create regression tests that verify:
   - Correct bias potential calculation
   - Accurate force derivatives
   - Proper restart behavior (if applicable)
   - Boundary condition handling

8. **Verification**: Run regression tests across different configurations (serial/MPI, different compiler flags).

## Next Steps

After mastering bias method implementation, consider exploring related advanced topics:

- **Creating Custom CVs**: Learn to implement new collective variables that your biases can operate on. See [Creating New CVs](24-creating-new-cvs) for the complementary development path.

- **Advanced Biasing Techniques**: Study complex bias methods like OPES, variational approaches, and maximum entropy methods. Refer to [Advanced Biasing Techniques](17-advanced-biasing-techniques) for architectural patterns.

- **Testing Framework**: Deepen understanding of PLUMED's regression testing infrastructure. See [Regression Testing Framework](27-regression-testing-framework) for comprehensive test design principles.

- **Performance Optimization**: Explore advanced optimization techniques for bias methods. See [Performance Optimization](30-performance-optimization) for systematic performance tuning approaches.

The bias method architecture provides a powerful framework for implementing virtually any enhanced sampling algorithm. By following the patterns and best practices outlined here, you can create robust, efficient, and maintainable bias methods that integrate seamlessly with the broader PLUMED ecosystem.

# Documentation and Doxygen



PLUMED employs a sophisticated multi-layered documentation architecture that integrates automatic code extraction with structured manual generation. The documentation system serves dual audiences: end-users requiring practical guidance for collective variable calculations and developers extending the framework through new actions and modules. This dual-track approach ensures that documentation evolves synchronously with code changes while maintaining clear separation between user-facing and developer-facing content.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L1-L20), [user-doc/Makefile](user-doc/Makefile#L1-L34)

## Documentation Architecture Overview

The documentation infrastructure comprises three interconnected documentation systems operating at different abstraction levels. The user documentation leverages Doxygen with custom processing to generate HTML pages that describe all available actions, collective variables, and command-line tools. Parallel to this, the developer documentation targets the C++ API and internal architecture for contributors extending PLUMED functionality. The new manual system represents an evolution toward Mkdocs-based documentation with modern theming and interactive features, designed to supersede the legacy Doxygen-based approach while maintaining compatibility with existing workflows.

This architecture implements a critical design principle: documentation is embedded directly within source code through specially formatted comment blocks, enabling automatic extraction and synchronization. When developers implement new actions, they are required to provide documentation through structured keyword registration and descriptive blocks, eliminating the possibility of undocumented functionality reaching users.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L20-L60), [new-manual/mkdocs.yml](new-manual/mkdocs.yml#L1-L57)

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Source Code"
        A[Action .cpp files<br/>with //+PLUMEDOC blocks]
        B[registerKeywords()<br/>method definitions]
        C[module.yml files<br/>with metadata]
    end

    subgraph "User Documentation Pipeline"
        D[extract script<br/>scans source files]
        E[Doxygen processing<br/>user-doc/Doxyfile]
        F[HTML generation<br/>with custom styling]
        G[Manual website<br/>plumed.org/doc]
    end

    subgraph "Developer Documentation Pipeline"
        H[go-doxygen<br/>developer-doc/]
        I[Developer Doxyfile<br/>API documentation]
        J[Developer HTML<br/>internal architecture]
    end

    subgraph "New Manual Pipeline"
        K[build_manual.py<br/>Python extraction]
        L[Mkdocs processing<br/>Material theme]
        M[Modern documentation<br/>with interactive features]
    end

    A --> D
    B --> D
    C --> D
    D --> E
    E --> F
    F --> G

    A --> H
    B --> H
    H --> I
    I --> J

    A --> K
    B --> K
    K --> L
    L --> M

    style G fill:#e1f5ff
    style J fill:#fff4e1
    style M fill:#f0e1ff
```

## Building User Documentation

The user documentation generation process begins with source code scanning through the `extract` script located in the `user-doc` directory. This script iterates through all C++ source files in `../src/*/*.cpp`, identifying actions registered with the `PLUMED_REGISTER_ACTION` macro and validating that each provides corresponding documentation through `PLUMEDOC` comment blocks. The extraction process generates intermediate files in an `automatic/` directory, creating glossary listings, module groupings, and individual action documentation pages that serve as input to Doxygen.

The `go-doxygen` shell script orchestrates the actual documentation generation by constructing a customized Doxygen configuration that incorporates the automatically extracted content with manually written pages. The script injects version information by querying the compiled PLUMED executable, ensuring that generated documentation accurately reflects the specific codebase version. Post-processing steps apply custom CSS styling through `plumed.css`, execute JavaScript transformations for interactive features via `plumed-syntax.awk`, and optionally generate PDF documentation through LaTeX compilation. The resulting HTML documentation provides comprehensive coverage of all PLUMED actions organized by module, with search capabilities and cross-references between related concepts.

Sources: [user-doc/extract](user-doc/extract#L1-L200), [user-doc/go-doxygen](user-doc/go-doxygen#L1-L146)

### Documentation Build Commands

Building the complete user documentation requires compilation of PLUMED itself, as the `extract` script queries the compiled executable for version information and available patch configurations. The standard build process executes through `make docs` when the `make_doc` configuration variable is enabled. This triggers the extraction pipeline followed by Doxygen generation, with optional PDF documentation controlled by the `make_pdfdoc` variable. Developers can check for broken examples or documentation errors using `make showerrors`, which executes the `report_errors` script to analyze generated documentation against the source code.

The build system validates documentation completeness by checking that every registered action has corresponding documentation, reporting violations to an errors file. It also extracts documentation for command-line tools by invoking each tool's `--description` and `--help` flags, automatically generating user-facing documentation for shell scripts and utilities. This comprehensive validation ensures that the generated documentation accurately represents the available functionality without orphaned or undocumented actions.

Sources: [user-doc/Makefile](user-doc/Makefile#L1-L34), [user-doc/extract](user-doc/extract#L200-L300)

## Building Developer Documentation

The developer documentation follows a streamlined build process designed for API and architectural documentation. The `developer-doc/go-doxygen` script configures Doxygen to process all C++ source files directly, targeting the internal codebase structure rather than the user-facing action documentation. This configuration disables reference relationship tracking to reduce generation time and focuses on class hierarchies, method signatures, and implementation details relevant to contributors extending PLUMED.

The developer Doxyfile is configured with output language set to English and UTF-8 encoding, with automatic extraction of documentation from source comments. Unlike the user documentation, this pipeline does not require intermediate extraction steps or post-processing, as the target audience requires direct access to code structure rather than the polished presentation needed by end users. The resulting documentation provides a complete API reference for internal classes, methods, and data structures that form the foundation of PLUMED's execution model.

Sources: [developer-doc/go-doxygen](developer-doc/go-doxygen#L1-L12), [developer-doc/Doxyfile](developer-doc/Doxyfile#L1-L100)

## In-Code Documentation Mechanism

The documentation system relies on structured comment blocks embedded directly within source code, enabling automatic extraction and synchronization. Actions must be documented using `//+PLUMEDOC` blocks that begin with the action name followed by optional tags for categorization. The comment block format follows GitHub-flavored markdown with PLUMED-specific extensions, supporting mathematical notation, bibliographic references, and HTML elements. The first paragraph serves as a brief description appearing in summary listings, while subsequent content provides detailed explanations for the dedicated action page.

Critical to the documentation philosophy is the integration with keyword registration through the static `registerKeywords` method. This method declares all input parameters, flags, and output values using the `PLMD::Keywords` interface, with each keyword requiring a descriptive explanation that becomes part of the generated documentation. Keywords support multiple attribute types: compulsory parameters requiring specification, optional parameters with default values, flags for boolean toggles, atom specifications, and numbered keyword sequences for repetitive parameters. The registration system enforces documentation completeness by preventing the parsing of undocumented keywords, creating a direct dependency between functionality and documentation.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L60-L120)

### Keyword Registration Patterns

The keyword registration system provides specialized methods for different parameter types, each with corresponding documentation requirements. Standard keywords use the `add()` method with attributes determining required/optional status and providing user-facing explanations. Input keywords that consume values from other actions utilize `addInputKeyword()`, which specifies acceptable types (scalar, vector, matrix, or grid) and enables type checking during input processing. Flags for boolean toggles employ `addFlag()` with default states, while numbered keyword sequences use `add()` with the numbered attribute to handle repetitions like `ATOM1`, `ATOM2`, `ATOM3`.

Output value documentation follows the same pattern through `setValueDescription()` and `addOutputComponent()` methods. These methods document the characteristics of values calculated by actions, distinguishing between scalar outputs and multi-component results accessible via dot notation. The registration system supports conditional components that appear only when specific keywords are present, with mechanisms to declare components as mandatory or optional based on action semantics. This comprehensive registration ensures that the generated documentation accurately reflects all available inputs and outputs with appropriate usage explanations.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L120-L250)

### Component Documentation Example

Actions generating multiple output values, such as those with the `COMPONENTS` keyword, must document each accessible component using `addOutputComponent()`. The method requires specifying the component name, the keyword that enables it, the value type, and a descriptive explanation. For actions that always generate specific components regardless of input configuration, the `componentsAreNotOptional()` method declares this behavior, simplifying component registration by removing keyword association requirements.

The MOVINGRESTRAINT action exemplifies this pattern, documenting bias and force2 components as always present while defining _cntr and _work components that scale with the number of input arguments. These component names combine argument names with descriptive suffixes, creating predictable output naming conventions. The registration system maps these documented components to actual calculation results, enabling users to reference individual outputs through the action label followed by component name.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L250-L300)

## Module Documentation System

PLUMED organizes actions into logical modules, each requiring two documentation files: `module.md` for descriptive content and `module.yml` for structured metadata. The markdown file provides module overview, usage guidance, and conceptual explanations using the same GitHub-flavored markdown syntax as action documentation. This content appears on the module's dedicated documentation page, offering context for understanding the collective purpose of actions within the module.

The YAML file contains structured metadata including module name, author list, description, DOI references for relevant publications, and tag definitions with explanations. Tags defined here become available for action categorization, enabling cross-module organization without rigid taxonomic constraints. Actions declare tag membership by including tag names on their `PLUMEDOC` line, creating flexible groupings that facilitate discovery of related functionality across module boundaries. This tag-based system supports community-driven organization, allowing contributors to define meaningful categories without restructuring the codebase.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L350-L438)

### Module YAML Structure

```yaml
name: module_identifier
authors: Author One, Author Two
description: Comprehensive description of module purpose
dois: ["doi:10.1234/example.doi", "doi:10.5678/another.doi"]
tags:
  DISTANCE: "Actions involving distance calculations"
  ANGLE: "Actions involving angle measurements"
  ENERGY: "Actions related to energy calculations"
```

The DOI references specified in module documentation enable automatic citation generation and linking to peer-reviewed publications, supporting PLUMED's philosophy that comprehensive documentation exists in the literature using the software. When actions are documented with `addDOI()` calls, citations automatically appear on action pages, connecting implementation details to the theoretical foundations published in research articles.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L300-L350)

## New Manual System

The `new-manual/` directory represents the next-generation documentation system built on Mkdocs with the Material theme, offering modern styling, dark mode support, and enhanced search capabilities. This system leverages Python scripts in `build_manual.py` to extract documentation from source code, processing action descriptions with parallel processing for efficiency and generating markdown files that Mkdocs compiles into static HTML. The system maintains compatibility with existing source documentation practices while providing a more flexible and maintainable foundation for future documentation evolution.

The Mkdocs configuration defines navigation structure linking to external tutorial resources on plumed-tutorials.org, integration with the PLUMED GitHub repository, and developer documentation hosted in a separate HTML tree. Custom CSS and JavaScript files extend the base theme with PLUMED-specific styling, table functionality through DataTables, mathematical rendering via MathJax, and diagram capabilities through Mermaid. This comprehensive toolset enables rich documentation with interactive examples, code snippets, and visual explanations that enhance user understanding of complex collective variable concepts.

Sources: [new-manual/build_manual.py](new-manual/build_manual.py#L1-L200), [new-manual/mkdocs.yml](new-manual/mkdocs.yml#L1-L57)

## Continuous Documentation Deployment

PLUMED implements automated documentation generation through Travis CI and GitHub Actions, ensuring that documentation stays synchronized with code changes. The continuous integration system builds documentation automatically on successful test completion, deploying to version-specific repositories under the plumed organization on GitHub. Each branch generates documentation at a corresponding repository URL, enabling version-aligned documentation that matches the specific codebase state.

The deployment mechanism handles version detection through environment variables, substituting branch names into documentation headers and navigation links. Coverage scans generate separate repositories containing regression test coverage data, providing transparency into which code paths are validated by automated tests. This automated pipeline eliminates manual documentation deployment steps while ensuring that only passing builds generate published documentation, preventing broken or incomplete documentation from reaching users.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L380-L438)

## Documentation Quality Assurance

The documentation build process includes multiple validation checks that detect common errors and inconsistencies. The extraction script identifies registered actions without corresponding documentation, reporting violations to an errors file for developer attention. Example testing validates that code snippets presented in documentation execute successfully without syntax errors or runtime failures. Spelling checks using a custom dictionary ensure consistent terminology and catch typos in user-facing text.

These quality assurance mechanisms operate during documentation generation rather than requiring separate validation steps, integrating documentation health checks into the standard development workflow. The `report_errors` script aggregates findings from multiple validation sources, presenting developers with actionable feedback on documentation completeness and accuracy. This comprehensive validation ensures that published documentation maintains high quality standards while minimizing additional overhead for contributors.

Sources: [user-doc/extract](user-doc/extract#L1-L50), [user-doc/report_errors](user-doc/report_errors), [user-doc/go-spelling](user-doc/go-spelling)

> [!TIP]
> The documentation system enforces completeness by requiring keyword registration before action input parsing, making it impossible to add undocumented parameters. This design ensures documentation evolves synchronously with code changes, preventing the common problem of orphaned functionality reaching users without corresponding documentation.

## Integration with External Resources

PLUMED documentation maintains extensive cross-referencing to external educational resources, particularly the PLUMED tutorials site (plumed-tutorials.org) and the PLUMED nest repository (plumed-nest.org). These connections support the documentation philosophy that practical examples and tutorials provide superior learning opportunities compared to comprehensive reference materials. Manual pages link to tutorials demonstrating specific calculations, while tutorial content references manual entries for detailed parameter explanations.

The bibliography system leverages DOIs to automatically generate citation information and links to peer-reviewed publications, connecting code implementation details to theoretical foundations. When actions document methods with `addDOI()` calls, the documentation system retrieves citation metadata from DOI resolution services, presenting formatted references alongside usage instructions. This integration ensures that users can trace the scientific basis of PLUMED functionality back to the original research publications, supporting reproducibility and proper citation in academic work.

Sources: [developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md](developer-doc/usingDoxygen.md#L1-L20)

## Next Steps

Understanding PLUMED's documentation architecture provides the foundation for effectively extending and maintaining the system. For practical experience implementing actions, refer to [Creating New CVs](24-creating-new-cvs) which demonstrates the registration and documentation patterns in concrete examples. The [Regression Testing Framework](27-regression-testing-framework) explains how to validate that your documented examples function correctly, while [Continuous Integration and Code Coverage](29-continuous-integration-and-code-coverage) describes how documentation quality checks integrate with automated testing.

For comprehensive understanding of PLUMED's action framework, the [Action Framework and Execution Model](6-action-framework-and-execution-model) provides the theoretical foundation for why documentation is structured around keyword registration and static initialization methods. When contributing to PLUMED, [How to Contribute to PLUMED](developer-doc/HowToContributeToPlumed.md) offers additional guidance on documentation standards and community expectations.

# Regression Testing Framework



The regression testing framework is a critical quality assurance system that ensures PLUMED's functionality remains stable across development. The framework automatically tests all code features and runs on every commit through continuous integration, making it an essential component of PLUMED's development workflow. Tests are organized by module and must be included for any new features to be considered for merging.

## Framework Architecture

The testing system follows a modular design that mirrors PLUMED's own module structure, with tests categorized by functionality rather than being in a monolithic collection.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[make tests] --> B[regtest/Makefile]
    B --> C[Discover all rt-*/Makefile]
    C --> D[Execute each test directory]
    D --> E[scripts/run - Execute Test]
    E --> F[scripts/check - Aggregate Results]
    F --> G[Final Report]
    
    subgraph Test Execution
        E --> E1[Check Dependencies]
        E1 --> E2[Run Test Type]
        E2 --> E3[Compare with Reference]
        E3 --> E4[Generate report.txt]
    end
    
    subgraph Test Types
        T1[driver]
        T2[simplemd]
        T3[sum_hills]
        T4[make]
        T5[python]
    end
    
    E2 --> T1
    E2 --> T2
    E2 --> T3
    E2 --> T4
    E2 --> T5
```

The framework operates through a hierarchical Makefile system. The top-level `regtest/Makefile` [regtest/Makefile#L1-L38](regtest/Makefile#L1-L38) discovers all test directories by locating `Makefile` files within `rt-*` directories, then executes each test. Results are aggregated and reported by scripts that examine the generated `report.txt` files in each test directory.

**Module Organization**: Tests are organized in subdirectories corresponding to PLUMED's modules:
- `basic/` - Core functionality tests
- `multicolvar/`, `bias/`, `colvar/` - Feature-specific tests
- `adjmat/`, `opes/`, `ves/` - Optional module tests
- `unittest/` - Unit tests for internal components

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L1-L59), [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200)

## Test Structure

Each regression test resides in its own directory following the naming convention `rt-*` and contains a standardized set of files.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Test Directory rt-*/] --> B[Makefile]
    A --> C[config]
    A --> D[plumed.dat]
    A --> E[*.reference files]
    A --> F[input files]
    F --> F1[trajectory.xyz]
    F --> F2[in]
    
    B --> G[include scripts/test.make]
    C --> H[Test configuration]
```

**Directory Contents**:
- `Makefile` - Single line including `../../scripts/test.make` [regtest/basic/rt0/Makefile#L1-L2](regtest/basic/rt0/Makefile#L1-L2)
- `config` - Configuration file defining test behavior
- `plumed.dat` - PLUMED input script for the test
- `*.reference` - Expected output files for comparison
- Input files (trajectories, coordinates, etc.)
- Generated files (report.txt, tmp/) are git-ignored

**Test Discovery**: The framework automatically identifies test directories by searching for `Makefile` files within directories matching the `rt-*` pattern [regtest/Makefile#L2](regtest/Makefile#L2). This convention allows new tests to be added without modifying the main Makefile.

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L1-L59), [regtest/scripts/test.make](regtest/scripts/test.make#L1-L18)

## Configuration System

The `config` file controls test execution through key-value pairs that define test type, requirements, and execution parameters.

| Parameter | Purpose | Example |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `type` | Test execution mode | `driver`, `simplemd`, `sum_hills`, `make`, `python` |
| `arg` | Command-line arguments | `"--plumed plumed.dat --timestep 0.05 trajectory.xyz"` |
| `mpiprocs` | MPI process count | `2` (defaults to 1 if not specified) |
| `plumed_modules` | Required optional modules | `adjmat`, `opes`, `ves` |
| `plumed_needs` | Required dependencies | `molfile`, `xdrfile` |
| `extra_files` | Files to copy from shared locations | `../../trajectories/trajectory.xyz` |

**Example Configuration** [regtest/basic/rt0/config#L1-L5](regtest/basic/rt0/config#L1-L5):
```bash
type=driver
arg="--plumed plumed.dat --trajectory-stride 10 --timestep 0.005 --ixyz trajectory.xyz --dump-forces forces --dump-forces-fmt=%8.4f --restart"
extra_files="../../trajectories/trajectory.xyz"
```

**MPI Configuration**: Tests requiring MPI specify `mpiprocs=N`. The framework automatically detects if MPI is available and marks tests as `NOT_APPLICABLE` if MPI is not installed, preventing CI failures on configurations without MPI [regtest/scripts/run#L50-L70](regtest/scripts/run#L50-L70).

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L1-L355)

## Test Types

The framework supports multiple execution modes tailored to different testing scenarios.

### Driver Tests
Uses `plumed driver` to analyze pre-computed trajectories. This is the most common test type for collective variables and biases.

**Execution**: `plumed driver --plumed plumed.dat --trajectory-stride N --timestep T --ixyz trajectory.xyz`

**Use Cases**:
- Testing collective variable calculations
- Validating bias methods on known trajectories
- Checking restart functionality

**Example** [regtest/basic/rt0/config](regtest/basic/rt0/config#L1-L5):
```bash
type=driver
arg="--plumed plumed.dat --trajectory-stride 10 --timestep 0.005 --ixyz trajectory.xyz --dump-forces forces --dump-forces-fmt=%8.4f"
```

### SimpleMD Tests
Runs Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics using PLUMED's built-in `simplemd` tool.

**Execution**: `plumed simplemd < in > out`

**Use Cases**:
- Testing integration with MD engines
- Validating forces and energy calculations
- End-to-end testing of PLUMED-in- workflows

**Example** [regtest/basic/rt-simplemd0/config](regtest/basic/rt-simplemd0/config#L1-L3):
```bash
type=simplemd
```

### Sum Hills Tests
Tests the `sum_hills` utility for processing metadynamics bias files.

**Use Cases**:
- Validating HILLS file processing
- Testing free energy reconstruction
- Checking bias grid operations

### Make Tests
Compiles and runs custom C++, Fortran, or C test programs linked against the PLUMED library. This mode supports multiple language variants and compilation configurations.

**Execution Flow** [regtest/scripts/run#L206-L254](regtest/scripts/run#L206-L254):
1. Generate Makefile with PLUMED configuration
2. Compile test program with appropriate flags
3. Execute compiled program with specified arguments

**Language Support**:
- C++ (default, C++98, C++11, C++14)
- Fortran (F77, F2008)
- C (C11)

**Use Cases**:
- Testing PLUMED API/Plugin interface
- Validating internal library functions
- Testing language bindings (Fortran, Python)

### Python Tests
Executes Python-based tests using the PLUMED Python module.

**Use Cases**:
- Testing Python interface
- Validating PLUMED operations from Python
- PyTorch integration tests

Sources: [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L1-L355), [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200)

## Test Execution Flow

The test execution process involves multiple stages managed by scripts.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as Developer
    participant Make as Makefile
    participant Run as scripts/run
    participant Test as Test Directory
    participant Check as scripts/check
    
    User->>Make: make tests
    Make->>Run: Execute each test directory
    Run->>Test: Create tmp/ directory
    Run->>Test: Read config
    Run->>Test: Copy extra_files
    Run->>Test: Execute test (driver/simplemd/make)
    Run->>Test: Compare output with *.reference
    Run->>Test: Write report.txt
    Check->>Test: Read all report.txt files
    Check->>User: Display aggregate results
```

**Execution Stages** [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L1-L355):

1. **Initialization**: Create `tmp/` directory and copy test files
2. **Dependency Checking**: Verify required modules and dependencies are available
3. **Test Execution**: Run the appropriate command based on `type`
4. **Output Comparison**: Compare generated files with `*.reference` files
5. **Report Generation**: Write results to `report.txt`

**Result Comparison** [regtest/scripts/run#L294-L332](regtest/scripts/run#L294-L332):
- Uses `diff` to compare output files with references
- Applies zero normalization via `fixzeroes.sh` script to handle minor numerical differences
- Marked as `FAILURE` if differences exceed tolerance
- Special handling for PLUMED field files (starting with `#! FIELDS`)

**Floating Point Tolerance**: The framework handles cross-platform numerical differences through:
- Explicit format specification in PLUMED inputs (`FMT=%8.4f`)
- Zero normalization (`-0.00` → ` 0.00`)
- NaN normalization (`-nan` → `nan`)

Sources: [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L1-L355), [regtest/scripts/fixzeroes.sh](regtest/scripts/fixzeroes.sh#L1-L14)

## Result Aggregation

After all tests execute, the `scripts/check` script aggregates results across all test directories.

**Checking Process** [regtest/scripts/check](regtest/scripts/check#L1-L87):
- Scans all `*/rt*/report.txt` files
- Categorizes results:
  - `OK` - Test passed
  - `FAILURE` - Test failed
  - `NOT_APPLICABLE` - Test skipped due to missing dependencies
- Generates summary report

**Output Format**:
```
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
+ Test session ended at [timestamp]
+ 500 tests performed, 5 tests not applicable
+ 0 errors found
+ Well done!!
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
```

**Continuous Integration**: Tests run automatically on every commit via Travis-CI/GitHub Actions across multiple architectures. The framework treats missing optional modules as non-fatal by marking relevant tests as `NOT_APPLICABLE` rather than failures.

**Coverage Reporting**: The `scripts/what` tool identifies PLUMED actions without corresponding tests by scanning registered actions and comparing against test inputs [regtest/scripts/what](regtest/scripts/what#L1-L22).

Sources: [regtest/scripts/check](regtest/scripts/check#L1-L87), [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200)

## Creating Tests

New regression tests must follow established conventions and be included with new features.

**Step-by-Step Process** [regtest/README](regtest/README#L1-L59):

1. **Create Test Directory**:
   ```bash
   mkdir regtest/module/rt-testname
   cd regtest/module/rt-testname
   ```

2. **Create Makefile**:
   ```bash
   echo "include ../../scripts/test.make" > Makefile
   ```

3. **Create config File** with appropriate parameters

4. **Add Input Files** (plumed.dat, trajectories)

5. **Run Test**:
   ```bash
   make
   ```

6. **Create Reference Files**:
   ```bash
   cp tmp/outputfile outputfile.reference
   ```

7. **Add to Git** (excluding tmp/ and report.txt):
   ```bash
   git add .
   git commit
   ```

**Best Practices**:
- Tests should complete in a few seconds
- Output files should be small
- Use explicit formatting (`FMT=%8.4f`) to ensure cross-platform consistency
- Test analytical derivatives against numerical derivatives during development, but commit only analytical derivatives to reference files
- Use shared trajectories from `regtest/trajectories/` to avoid duplication

> [!TIP]
> When testing new collective variables inheriting from PLMD::Colvar, PLMD::function::Function, or PLMD::multicolvar::MultiColvarBase, use the DUMPDERIVATIVES action to compare analytical and numerical derivatives during development. However, only commit the analytical derivatives to reference files, as numerical derivatives vary across architectures.

**Testing Pattern for CVs** [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L130-L150):
```plumed
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2
d1n: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2 NUMERICAL_DERIVATIVES
PRINT ARG=d1 FILE=colvar FMT=%8.4f
DUMPDERIVATIVES ARG=d1,d1n FILE=deriv FMT=%8.4f
```

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L1-L59), [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200)

## Test Maintenance

Tests require periodic updates when behavior changes or numerical tolerances shift.

**Updating References**:
```bash
cd regtest/module/rt-testname
make reset
```

The `make reset` command [regtest/scripts/reset](regtest/scripts/reset#L1-L9) automatically copies current output files to replace reference files when intentional changes have been made to functionality.

**Debugging Failed Tests**:
1. Check `report.txt` in the test directory for detailed error messages
2. Examine `tmp/` directory for actual output
3. Review diff output showing differences
4. Verify test configuration (type, dependencies, arguments)
5. Check if all required modules are installed

**Valgrind Testing**:
```bash
make valgrind
```

Runs tests with Valgrind memory checking to detect leaks and memory errors. Note that MPI tests cannot be run with Valgrind [regtest/scripts/run#L72-L85](regtest/scripts/run#L72-L85).

Sources: [regtest/scripts/reset](regtest/scripts/reset#L1-L9), [regtest/scripts/valgrind](regtest/scripts/test.make#L11-L14)

## Shared Resources

The framework provides shared resources to avoid duplication and maintain consistency.

**Trajectory Repository** [regtest/trajectories/](regtest/trajectories/):
- Common trajectory files used across multiple tests
- Includes various formats (xyz, xtc, trr, gro)
- Organized by use case (pca/, rmsd/, path_msd/)

**Configuration Files**:
- PLUMED module configuration checks dependencies
- Module availability validation before test execution

**Custom Skip Logic**:
Tests can define `plumed_custom_skip()` functions in their config to implement custom skipping logic for specific conditions.

Sources: [regtest/trajectories/](regtest/trajectories/), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L120-L145)

## Continuous Integration

The regression test suite is integrated with automated CI systems.

**CI Platforms**:
- Travis-CI: Continuous testing on commit
- GitHub Actions: Modern CI integration
- Multiple architectures tested simultaneously

**CI Behavior** [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L55-L85):
- Tests requiring unavailable dependencies are marked `NOT_APPLICABLE`
- MPI tests skip gracefully on non-MPI configurations
- Valgrind testing excluded for MPI tests
- Environment variable `PLUMED_ALLOW_SKIP_ON_TRAVIS` can override strict checking

**Quality Policy**: PLUMED developers take testing seriously and will not merge contributions without appropriate regression tests [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L10-L12).

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L200), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L1-L355)

The regression testing framework provides a robust, modular system for ensuring PLUMED's stability and correctness. By understanding its architecture, test types, and conventions, developers can effectively contribute new tests and maintain existing ones, ensuring PLUMED remains reliable across platforms and versions.

For detailed guidance on writing specific types of tests, continue to [Writing Regression Tests](28-writing-regression-tests). To understand how the testing framework integrates with broader quality assurance practices, see [Continuous Integration and Code Coverage](29-continuous-integration-and-code-coverage).

# Writing Regression Tests



Regression tests are the foundation of PLUMED's quality assurance system, ensuring that new code contributions don't break existing functionality while validating that new features work correctly across different architectures and configurations. The testing framework is designed for automated execution during development and continuous integration, with tests running on multiple platforms whenever code is pushed to the repository.

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L20), [regtest/README](regtest/README#L1-L10)

## Test Framework Architecture

The PLUMED regression testing system operates as a hierarchical framework where individual test modules execute independently under a unified management layer. Tests are organized into directories that roughly correspond to PLUMED's functional modules, with each test directory containing everything needed for execution and validation.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[make tests] --> B[regtest/Makefile]
    B --> C[Scan rt-*/ directories]
    C --> D[Execute each test]
    D --> E[scripts/run test execution]
    E --> F[Compare with .reference files]
    F --> G[scripts/check aggregate results]
    G --> H{All tests pass?}
    H -->|Yes| I[SUCCESS]
    H -->|No| J[FAILURE - review report.txt]
```

The test runner script handles all aspects of test execution including environment setup, dependency checking, MPI configuration, and output comparison. When you execute `make tests` from the regtest directory, the system automatically discovers all test directories matching the `rt-*` pattern and runs them sequentially or in parallel depending on your build configuration.

Sources: [regtest/Makefile](regtest/Makefile#L1-L38), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L1-L50), [regtest/scripts/check](regtest/scripts/check#L1-L30)

## Creating a New Regression Test

### Test Directory Structure

Every regression test requires a dedicated directory named with the `rt-*` prefix, where the wildcard portion should provide a descriptive indication of what feature is being tested. The naming convention is mandatory as the build system uses pattern matching to identify test directories.

The complete test directory structure requires:
- `config` - Configuration file defining test parameters
- `Makefile` - Standard test execution script
- `plumed.dat` - PLUMED input file
- `[filename].reference` - Reference output files for comparison
- Supporting files (trajectories, PDB files, etc.)

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L30-L40), [regtest/README](regtest/README#L15-L25)

### Configuration File Options

The `config` file controls how your test executes and what dependencies it requires. Configuration parameters are simple key-value pairs that define test behavior:

| Parameter | Description | Required | Example |
|-----------|-------------|----------|---------|
| `type` | Test execution mode | Yes | `driver`, `simplemd`, `sum_hills`, `make` |
| `arg` | Command line arguments | For driver type | `"--plumed=plumed.dat --timestep=0.05 trajectory.xyz"` |
| `mpiprocs` | Number of MPI processes | Optional, defaults to 1 | `2`, `4`, `8` |
| `plumed_modules` | Required PLUMED modules | For optional features | `adjmat`, `colvar` |
| `plumed_needs` | Required dependencies | For external features | `xdrfile`, `molfile` |
| `extra_files` | Files to copy from shared locations | Optional | `"../../trajectories/trajectory.xyz"` |

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L45-L75), [regtest/README](regtest/README#L15-L25)

### Test Types and Their Use Cases

The framework supports four primary test types, each suited for different testing scenarios:

| Type | Use Case | Input Files | Execution Method |
|------|----------|-------------|------------------|
| `driver` | Trajectory analysis and CV calculation | `plumed.dat`, trajectory file | `plumed driver` command |
| `simplemd` | Full molecular dynamics simulation | `in`, `input.xyz`, `plumed.dat` | Built-in LJ MD engine |
| `sum_hills` | Hills file processing and free energy reconstruction | `plumed.dat`, hills files | `plumed sum_hills` utility |
| `make` | Custom C++/Fortran test programs | `main.cpp`, `plumed.dat` | Compile and link to PLUMED library |

The `driver` type is most common as it allows testing collective variables and biases by analyzing pre-computed trajectories without the computational cost of running MD simulations. The `simplemd` type is useful when you need to verify that your CV or bias works correctly in a dynamic simulation context.

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L55-L70), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L200-L230)

## Test Execution Workflow

### Step-by-Step Process

Creating and validating a regression test follows a systematic workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Create rt-xxx directory] --> B[Write config and Makefile]
    B --> C[Create plumed.dat input]
    C --> D[Add supporting files]
    D --> E[Run make to execute test]
    E --> F[Examine tmp/ output]
    F --> G[Create .reference files]
    G --> H[Re-run to verify]
    H --> I{Tests pass?}
    I -->|No| J[Debug and fix issues]
    J --> E
    I -->|Yes| K[Commit to git repository]
```

The execution process creates a temporary `tmp` directory containing all generated output files. This separation ensures clean test runs and prevents reference file contamination. After successful execution, you copy output files from `tmp/` to the test directory with `.reference` appended to the filename.

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L30-L45), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L260-L355)

### Creating Reference Files

Reference files serve as the gold standard for test validation. The comparison system performs exact byte-by-byte matching with some tolerance for minor numerical variations. When creating reference files:

1. Run the test once with `make` inside your test directory
2. Examine the output in the `tmp/` directory
3. Copy relevant output files to the parent directory with `.reference` suffix
4. Example: `cp tmp/COLVAR COLVAR.reference`

The testing framework automatically compares each generated file against its reference counterpart. Any difference beyond the normal numerical tolerance results in a test failure. The system uses a `fixzeroes.sh` script to normalize floating-point representations, handling differences like `-0.0` versus `0.0`.

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L40-L50), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L320-L355), [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L80-L95)

## Testing Collective Variables and Derivatives

### Analytical vs. Numerical Derivatives

For collective variables that inherit from `PLMD::Colvar`, `PLMD::function::Function`, or `PLMD::multicolvar::MultiColvarBase`, validate derivative correctness by comparing analytical and numerical derivatives during test development:

```plumed
# Test analytical derivatives
d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2

# Test numerical derivatives (for validation only)
d1n: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2 NUMERICAL_DERIVATIVES

# Output both for comparison during development
DUMPDERIVATIVES ARG=d1,d1n FILE=deriv FMT=%8.4f

PRINT ARG=d1 FILE=colvar FMT=%8.4f
```

During initial development, compare columns 3 (analytical) and 4 (numerical) of the derivative file using `awk '{print $3-$4}' tmp/deriv`. Once you've verified they match, **commit only the analytical derivatives** to the repository. This approach avoids cross-platform numerical instability issues while ensuring derivative correctness.

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L100-L145)

> [!TIP]
> Always use explicit `FMT` specifications when outputting floating-point numbers in tests. Different compilers and architectures produce slightly different floating-point representations, and explicit formatting ensures consistent output across platforms. Use formats like `FMT=%8.4f` rather than default formatting.

### Complex Features with Bias Forces

For more complex features involving custom apply methods or multi-step CV calculations, validate force correctness using the `--debug-forces` option:

```bash
plumed driver --ixyz trajectory.xyz --debug-forces forces.num
```

This generates a three-column file: atom index, analytical forces, and numerically computed forces. The numerical calculation is computationally expensive and **should not be included in committed tests**. Instead, commit only the analytical forces using the standard `--dump-forces` option:

```bash
plumed driver --ixyz trajectory.xyz --dump-forces forces --dump-forces-fmt %8.4f
```

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L150-L190)

## Advanced Test Configuration

### MPI Testing

For parallel features, configure MPI execution using the `mpiprocs` parameter:

```config
mpiprocs=4
type=driver
arg="--plumed=plumed.dat --timestep=0.05 --ixyz trajectory.xyz"
extra_files="../../trajectories/trajectory.xyz"
```

The test framework automatically handles MPI detection and will skip the test gracefully if MPI is not available. This ensures tests don't fail on systems without MPI support while still validating parallel functionality where available.

Sources: [regtest/basic/rt-mpi0/config](regtest/basic/rt-mpi0/config#L1-L6), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L70-L100)

### Module-Specific Tests

When testing features from optional modules, specify module dependencies:

```config
type=driver
plumed_modules=adjmat
arg="--plumed plumed.dat --trajectory-stride 50 --timestep 0.005 --ixyz diala_traj_nm.xyz"
extra_files="../../trajectories/diala_traj_nm.xyz"
```

The framework checks module availability before execution and marks tests as "NOT_APPLICABLE" if required modules aren't installed. This prevents false test failures in minimal builds.

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L60-L75), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L100-L120)

## File Sharing and Organization

### Shared Trajectories

To minimize repository size, PLUMED maintains a shared trajectory directory at `regtest/trajectories/`. Reference these files using relative paths in your config:

```config
extra_files="../../trajectories/trajectory.xyz"
```

The test runner automatically copies these files to the temporary execution directory before running the test. This approach allows multiple tests to use the same trajectory without duplication.

Sources: [regtest/trajectories/](regtest/trajectories/), [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L50-L60)

### Test Organization by Module

Organize tests logically within the regtest hierarchy:
- `regtest/basic/` - Core functionality tests
- `regtest/adjmat/` - Adjacency matrix module tests
- `regtest/colvar/` - Collective variable specific tests
- `regtest/bias/` - Bias method tests
- Module-specific directories for optional features

This organization makes tests easier to locate and maintain, while allowing targeted test execution during development.

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L25-L35)

## Running and Debugging Tests

### Executing Individual Tests

Run specific tests during development:

```bash
cd regtest/basic/rt-mytest
make
```

This executes just your test and creates a `report.txt` file with detailed results. Examine the `tmp/` directory to inspect output files and identify issues.

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L30-L35), [regtest/scripts/test.make](regtest/scripts/test.make#L1-L10)

### Updating Reference Files

When you need to update reference files after legitimate code changes:

```bash
cd regtest/basic/rt-mytest
make reset
```

This command regenerates all `.reference` files from the current test output. Commit the updated references after verifying they are correct.

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L52-L55), [regtest/scripts/reset](regtest/scripts/test.make#L3-L4)

### Full Test Suite Execution

Run the complete regression test suite:

```bash
cd regtest
make tests              # Run all tests sequentially
make -j 4 tests         # Run 4 tests in parallel
make valgrind           # Run with memory leak detection
```

The `scripts/check` script aggregates results from all tests and provides a summary report showing the number of passed, failed, and skipped tests.

Sources: [regtest/README](regtest/README#L10-L15), [regtest/Makefile](regtest/Makefile#L1-L20), [regtest/scripts/check](regtest/scripts/check#L40-L80)

## Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

> [!TIP]
> Keep tests fast and small. Tests should complete in seconds rather than minutes. Use short trajectory files (10-100 frames) and minimize the number of collective variables calculated. This keeps the development cycle efficient and ensures CI systems run quickly.

### Essential Guidelines

1. **Always use FMT specifications** for numerical output to ensure cross-platform consistency
2. **Commit only analytical derivatives** - numerical derivatives are for validation only
3. **Keep tests focused** - test one feature or concept per test directory
4. **Use shared trajectories** when possible to reduce repository size
5. **Check module dependencies** - specify `plumed_modules` for optional features
6. **Validate on multiple architectures** - tests should pass on different compilers and platforms

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L20), [regtest/basic/rt0/plumed.dat](regtest/basic/rt0/plumed.dat#L1-L41)

### Common Issues and Solutions

| Issue | Cause | Solution |
|-------|-------|----------|
| Test passes locally but fails on CI | Platform-specific numerical differences | Use explicit FMT formatting, reduce precision requirements |
| Reference file changes unexpectedly | Floating point representation variations | Run `make reset` on the target platform |
| MPI tests skip unnecessarily | MPI not detected in CI environment | Check CI configuration, ensure MPI is available |
| Module tests marked NOT_APPLICABLE | Module not enabled in build | Verify `plumed_modules` specification, rebuild with module |

Sources: [regtest/scripts/run](regtest/scripts/run#L70-L140), [regtest/scripts/check](regtest/scripts/check#L50-L80)

## Integration with Development Workflow

Regression tests are mandatory for code contributions. The development team considers code without appropriate tests incomplete and will not merge contributions without test coverage. Tests run automatically on every push to the main repository through continuous integration systems.

After creating your feature and corresponding test:

```bash
cd regtest
git add rt-mynewtest
git commit -m "Add regression test for new feature"
```

This ensures your test becomes part of the permanent test suite, protecting your feature from future regressions and providing documentation of expected behavior.

Sources: [developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md](developer-doc/AddingRegressionTests.md#L1-L20), [regtest/README](regtest/README#L45-L55)

Now that you understand how to write regression tests, explore these related topics:
